articles.title: Instagram is giving schools a faster way to get students’ posts taken down
articles.summary: Instagram is rolling out a new school partnership program that will automatically prioritize reports made by educational institutions.
articles.body: Instagram is rolling out a new program to fast-track moderation reports made by school districts. After a district joins the new Schools Partnership program, any post or account they flag for potentially violating Instagram’s rules will “be automatically prioritized for review.” The school’s account will then receive notifications about the status of their report, and whether Instagram takes action on it. The partnership program is available to middle schools and high schools in the US, and it will allow them to take action against harmful content students may post. [Image: School partners will have a banner on their profile. Schools are often made aware of threats or inappropriate content posted on social media platforms, and some use monitoring programs to keep tabs on what students post online. Educational institutions will get a banner on their profile indicating that they’re part of the program, and they’ll gain access to resources to “help support educators, parents, guardians and students navigate Instagram safely.” Instagram has been trying to get ahead of the online child safety legislation popping up across the US. Last year, Instagram moved teens into more private accounts and began using AI to scan for signals that someone might be lying about their age. It also partnered with the nonprofit organization Childhelp to develop a curriculum that teaches middle schoolers how to recognize online exploitation, including sextortion scams and grooming.

articles.title: Cloudflare shows internet outages aren’t a matter of if — but when
articles.summary: The latest Cloudflare outage draws attention to concentration in the web infrastructure industry, with one expert saying it should serve as a “wake-up call” for companies.
articles.body: Cloudflare has become the latest web infrastructure giant to collapse in the span of a month, replacing entire sites, including X, ChatGPT, Spotify, Canva, and even the outage-tracking Downdetector, with an error message for hours this morning. It’s the latest in a string of outages that Mehdi Daoudi, CEO and cofounder of the internet performance monitoring platform Catchpoint, says should be a “wake-up call” for companies. “Everybody’s putting all their eggs in one basket, and then they’re surprised when there is a problem,” Daoudi says. “It’s on the company’s side to make sure that they have redundancy and resiliency.” The outage comes after issues affecting Microsoft Azure and Amazon Web Services occurred within just one week of each other, bringing down large chunks of the internet that rely on major providers to keep their websites running. Cloudflare similarly powers a sizable part of the internet. It keeps websites online with its content delivery network, while offering several other services, including DDoS attack protection and DNS. Last year, the company said around 20 percent of the web runs through Cloudflare’s network. It also serves 35 percent of companies on the Fortune 500 list, in addition to “millions” of other customers. Cloudflare’s speedy performance and security record make it a popular choice for websites across the globe, but this latest outage draws attention to just how concentrated the web infrastructure industry has become. After the AWS outage took down the secure messaging app Signal, the service’s president, Meredith Whittaker, said the company didn’t have any other choice but to use a major cloud service provider to run on. “The entire stack, practically speaking, is owned by 3-4 players,” she wrote. But even with companies relying on just a few web infrastructure providers, the last chain of outages makes it clear that they need a backup plan. “Outages will be here, and they’re just going to keep happening more frequently. The blast radius will keep growing,” Daoudi tells The Verge. “The question is, what are you doing about it?” Though Microsoft and AWS linked their outages to issues related to DNS — a system that translates website domain names into IP addresses — Cloudflare traced its outage to a single file. “The root cause of the outage was a configuration file that is automatically generated to manage threat traffic,” Cloudflare spokesperson Jackie Dutton said. “The file grew beyond an expected size of entries and triggered a crash in the software system that handles traffic for a number of Cloudflare’s services.” It may seem absurd that a file issue like this could bring down swaths of the internet, but for companies as large as Cloudflare, it can happen. “When you operate infrastructure at Cloudflare’s scale, even small deviations can have outsized consequences,” Rob Lee, the chief of AI and research at the SANS Institute, tells The Verge. “These platforms are built for speed, so anything that delays or halts decision-making can cascade quickly. In high performance environments, a millisecond delay can become a complete traffic stoppage.” According to Lee, a configuration file like the one Cloudflare describes “drives routing security policies, load balancing decisions, and how traffic is distributed globally.” If the file suddenly increases in size, “it can trigger slower parsing, memory issues, CPU contention, or logic failures inside the systems that rely on it,” Lee adds. AWS similarly blamed “faulty automation” for setting off a chain of issues that led to its most recent widespread outage — the kind of error that’s bound to happen again. “Are you going to complain about it every time Cloudflare sneezes?” Daoudi says. “Or are you going to build around it?”

articles.title: Google ordered to open Android and Search to rivals in Europe
articles.summary: The EU says Google must let rival search engines and AI assistants have comparable access to Android and some Search data to comply with the DMA.
articles.body: Google must give rival AI assistants and search engines greater access to key parts of Android and Google Search after the European Union ordered the company to comply with the bloc’s digital antitrust rules. The two decisions, handed down Thursday, could weaken Google’s control over two of the tech industry’s most important platforms and have far-reaching consequences for the company, shape the future of its AI tool Gemini, and open up new opportunities for rivals to gain ground. Google has until January 2027 to begin sharing search data and July 2027 to implement changes to Android. The rulings stem from technical regulatory proceedings under the EU’s Digital Markets Act (DMA), which requires dominant platforms — designated “gatekeepers” — to give competitors comparable access to systems and data as they themselves enjoy. Unlike a financial penalty, the procedures require Google to change how it operates in order to bring its services in line with the DMA and are developed through extensive engagement between the company and regulators. If Google does not comply, the European Commission could impose fines of up to 10 percent of its annual worldwide turnover, potentially tens of billions of dollars. The two proceedings focus on separate but thematically similar parts of Google’s business: How rival AI assistants can operate on Android, and how competing search engines and other AI chatbots can access data generated by Google Search. The Android decision sets out how Google must give rival AI assistants the same kind of system features and data access as it gives Gemini. In practical terms, it requires greater interoperability, allowing users — rather than Google — to decide whether competing tools can access their data and device hardware. That could include the ability to interact with apps, respond to voice commands like “Hey Google,” and make fuller use of the phone’s hardware. That means Android users could eventually choose ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity, or other assistants as deeply integrated system assistants instead of Gemini, with comparable access to device capabilities. The second proceeding focuses on Google Search and the data it generates, setting out how competing search engines and AI services can gain access to information historically kept by Google. Notably, the EU said this includes AI chatbots, which effectively function as search engines in some cases. The data-sharing measure broadly echoes remedies ordered in the US search antitrust case, where Google was instructed to share valuable search information with rivals that could help boost their ability to compete. Google has pushed back against both of these measures, arguing the requirements pose an unacceptable risk to user privacy and security, as well as compromise its products. The EU said there will be limits on how search data can be used and that Google will be able to vet which services get deeper access to Android to ensure safety and security aren’t compromised. Today’s rulings may also offer an indication into how Brussels will approach similar questions involving other tech giants. This includes Apple, which declined to release Siri AI in Europe, explicitly blaming the DMA and arguing its interoperability requirements compromise user safety. “With today’s measures, we want to support innovation and diversity in the European Union, enabling fair competition in the markets of AI assistant for Android devices and search engines,” said European Commission executive vice president for tech sovereignty, security, and democracy Henna Virkkunen. “Thanks to these measures we hope to see emerging alternatives to Google Search and Google’s AI services, such as Gemini, and that users in the EU can enjoy greater choice of services. All developers, large and small, are welcome to explore these new opportunities, which will certainly benefit users too.” In a blog post published after the decisions, Google’s president of global affairs Kent Walker said: “Today’s decisions risk undermining vital privacy and security guardrails for millions of Europeans. We have repeatedly offered solutions to safeguard users while satisfying the DMA’s goals, but these rulings discount extensive evidence of user harm.”

articles.title: Vai trabalhar no dia da eleição? Veja seus direitos  | G1
articles.standfirst: Direito vale para trabalhadores de todas as categorias, inclusive quem precisa se deslocar para outra cidade para votar. Veja o que a empresa pode e não pode fazer.
articles.summary: Direito vale para trabalhadores de todas as categorias, inclusive quem precisa se deslocar para outra cidade para votar. Veja o que a empresa pode e não pode fazer.
articles.body:
Urnas eletrônicas 2024 do Paraná — Foto: Giuliano Gomes/PR Press

Para milhões de brasileiros, o primeiro turno das eleições também será dia de expediente. Profissionais da saúde, da segurança, da hotelaria e de outros serviços essenciais precisarão conciliar a jornada de trabalho com a ida às urnas.

É nesse momento que surgem dúvidas recorrentes como: a empresa é obrigada a liberar o funcionário para votar? O tempo utilizado pode ser descontado do salário? É preciso compensar essas horas depois?

A legislação brasileira garante ao trabalhador o direito de se ausentar pelo tempo necessário para votar, sem sofrer qualquer prejuízo.

⚠️ O empregador não pode criar obstáculos ao deslocamento nem adotar medidas que dificultem o exercício desse direito. Isso inclui descontos no salário ou a exigência de compensar as horas utilizadas para comparecer à seção eleitoral.

Para ajudar quem estará de expediente durante a votação, o g1 reuniu as principais dúvidas sobre a legislação eleitoral e os direitos dos trabalhadores no dia da eleição.

Quem trabalha no dia da eleição pode sair para votar?

Sim. O trabalhador tem o direito de se ausentar pelo tempo necessário para ir ao local de votação e votar. A empresa não pode impedir esse deslocamento nem criar dificuldades que inviabilizem o exercício desse direito.

Essa garantia vale para qualquer categoria profissional. O direito é o mesmo para quem trabalha em hospital, supermercado, restaurante, fábrica, posto de combustível ou qualquer outro estabelecimento que funcione aos domingos.

Na prática, o empregador deve organizar a jornada para que o trabalhador consiga exercer seu direito ao voto.

O patrão é obrigado a liberar o funcionário?

O Ministério Público do Trabalho (MPT) determina que o empregador deve permitir que o funcionário se ausente pelo tempo necessário para ir à seção eleitoral, votar e retornar ao trabalho.

A regra vale mesmo quando a empresa está com grande movimento ou quando o trabalhador está escalado em horário coincidente com a votação.

As horas usadas para votar podem ser descontadas?

Não. O período necessário para ir às urnas não pode resultar em descontos no salário do trabalhador.

A empresa também não pode exigir a compensação das horas utilizadas para votar. De acordo com o MPT, esse tipo de exigência pode dificultar o exercício de um direito garantido pela legislação eleitoral.

Em outras palavras, o funcionário não precisa repor esse tempo depois nem acumular horas negativas por ter comparecido à sua seção eleitoral.

Nesses casos, a proteção continua valendo. O empregador não pode criar obstáculos ao exercício do voto, mesmo quando o trabalhador precisa viajar para outra cidade para votar.

Isso não significa que qualquer ausência será automática ou sem limites. O que a legislação protege é o exercício do direito ao voto. Por isso, a empresa deve ajustar a jornada de trabalho para permitir que o trabalhador vote.

E se a empresa dificultar a ida às urnas?

O Código Eleitoral estabelece que ninguém pode impedir ou dificultar o exercício do voto. Criar obstáculos ao comparecimento às urnas pode configurar uma infração eleitoral.

Isso vale tanto para situações explícitas quanto para formas indiretas de dificultar a votação.

alterar escalas para dificultar a votação;

criar constrangimentos relacionados à ida às urnas.

Também são consideradas práticas irregulares situações como:

exigir que o funcionário informe sua preferência eleitoral;

determinar que o trabalhador grave ou fotografe o momento da votação.

E conversar sobre política no trabalho? É proibido?

A legislação não proíbe conversas sobre política. O problema surge quando o ambiente de trabalho é usado para pressionar ou constranger alguém por causa de suas opiniões políticas.

O MPT destaca que empregadores não podem utilizar sua posição hierárquica para influenciar o voto dos funcionários.

Quando a situação passa a ser assédio eleitoral?

O assédio eleitoral ocorre quando há ameaças, constrangimentos, humilhações, intimidação ou promessa de vantagens com o objetivo de influenciar a escolha política do trabalhador.

Entre os exemplos citados na cartilha estão:

ameaças de demissão ligadas ao resultado das eleições;

promessas de benefícios em troca de apoio político;

pressão para participar de atos de campanha;

exigência do uso de roupas, adesivos ou materiais ligados a candidatos;

perseguição de trabalhadores por suas opiniões políticas.

Quem enfrentar dificuldades para votar ou sofrer pressão relacionada às eleições deve guardar provas sempre que possível, aponta o MPT.

Mensagens de WhatsApp, e-mails, vídeos, áudios, prints de conversas, documentos e testemunhos podem ajudar a comprovar os fatos.

As denúncias podem ser encaminhadas ao Ministério Público do Trabalho , ao Ministério Público Eleitoral (MPE) e aos canais de denúncia dos Tribunais Regionais do Trabalho .

O trabalhador também pode procurar o sindicato da categoria para receber orientação e apoio.

articles.title: Plataforma de transporte é condenada após passageiro sofrer acidente | G1
articles.standfirst: Juizado Especial Cível, Criminal e da Fazenda Pública determinou pagamento de R$ 4 mil por danos morais e restituição de R$ 27,60 cobrados por corrida que não foi concluída.
articles.summary: Passageiro sofreu acidente durante corrida de moto em Parnamirim. Plataforma terá de pagar R$ 4 mil por danos morais e devolver R$ 27,60.
articles.body:
O 1º Juizado Especial Cível, Criminal e da Fazenda Pública da Comarca de Parnamirim condenou uma plataforma de transporte por aplicativo a indenizar um passageiro que sofreu um acidente durante uma corrida de motocicleta. A empresa também deverá devolver R$ 27,60 cobrados pelo trajeto, que não foi concluído.

O acidente aconteceu em março de 2026, durante uma corrida contratada pelo aplicativo. Segundo o processo, o motociclista trafegava entre um veículo e o meio-fio quando a porta de um carro que estava parado para o desembarque de um passageiro foi aberta. A colisão provocou o acidente.

O passageiro afirmou ainda que, mesmo sem chegar ao destino, foi cobrado pelo valor da corrida.

A plataforma argumentou que não poderia ser responsabilizada pelos atos do motociclista porque ele trabalhava de forma autônoma e não possuía vínculo com a empresa. A empresa também defendeu que o Código de Defesa do Consumidor (CDC) não deveria ser aplicado ao caso.

A juíza Leila Nunes Pereira, no entanto, entendeu que a empresa integra a cadeia de fornecimento do serviço de transporte oferecido pela plataforma. Com isso, reconheceu a existência de uma relação de consumo e aplicou a responsabilidade objetiva prevista no artigo 14 do CDC.

Na sentença, a magistrada afirmou que o acidente ocorrido durante o trajeto contratado é considerado um "fortuito interno", relacionado aos riscos da atividade da empresa. Segundo ela, isso não afasta a responsabilidade da plataforma pelos danos causados pela falha na prestação do serviço.

Para a juíza, a falha ficou caracterizada pela condução inadequada do motociclista credenciado à plataforma e pela cobrança da corrida, mesmo após o trajeto ter sido interrompido pelo acidente.

A magistrada também considerou que a situação ultrapassou um mero aborrecimento, levando em conta o acidente e a cobrança posterior.

A plataforma foi condenada a devolver os R$ 27,60 pagos pela corrida, a título de danos materiais, e a pagar R$ 4 mil por danos morais. Os valores ainda terão correção monetária e incidência de juros.

articles.title: Shifting Senate Map Is Fueling Most Expensive US Election Ever
articles.summary: The political battle for the Senate is spreading to states many analysts doubted would have a central role in the November midterms, prompting both parties t...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- The political battle for the Senate is spreading to states many analysts doubted would have a central role in the November midterms, prompting both parties to bolster spending in an election that is on track to be the most expensive in American history.

Just 36 days before Election Day, and with voting underway in almost half the country, Democrats are betting that voter frustration with the cost-of-living can outpace the Republican Party's financial arsenal. An estimated $11.6 billion has been spent so far, according to the ad tracking website AdImpact. That's more than was spent during the entire 2024 presidential race.

On the Senate side, this year's midterms initially looked to favor Republicans, given the number of states where Democratic incumbents were both on the ballot and seen as at-risk following President Donald Trump's 2024 election. But recent weeks have seen Democrats leading or making gains in states previously viewed as long shots, including Iowa, Kansas, Alaska, Ohio and even Texas. Democrats need to flip four seats to take a majority.

"As the trend lines start to come into view, they have everybody thinking this is genuinely a toss-up. There are so many close races," says Kevin Madden, a GOP strategist who now advises companies.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report rates seven Senate races as "toss-ups." Kansas, which hasn't elected a Democratic senator since Franklin Delano Roosevelt's administration nearly a century ago, is listed as "lean Republican," a stunning shift in a state Trump won two years ago by 16 percentage points.

Republican anxiety about the state of the race nationally has been clear in recent weeks, as GOP lawmakers began pushing back on the administration's failure to resolve the war in Iran, its deportation policies and the cost of living. Those moves came as mortgage rates spiked above 7%, the White House tried to ban several media outlets and Trump hosted Chinese President Xi Jinping for meetings that were heavy on pomp and light on substance.

And while the White House says Trump will begin an intense series of campaign-style rallies for Republicans in the final weeks before the midterms, when he has traveled lately he's mostly visited deep red states and districts. The next two trips on his calendar, the White House said, are Oklahoma and Alabama, states overwhelmingly dominated by the GOP.
authors: Nancy Cook, Bill Allison, Catherine Lucey and Amanda Gordon

articles.title: US and China agree to cut tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods, from coal to toys
articles.summary: The United States and China have agreed to slash tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods, deepening efforts to stabilize a frequently testy relationship.
articles.body:
The United States and China have agreed to slash tariffs on $60 billion worth of goods, deepening efforts to stabilize a frequently testy relationship.

The tariff relief extends to an array of products, from US coal and agricultural products to made-in-China toys, car seats and holiday decorations.

The announcement from the White House late Sunday followed a highly anticipated meeting between US President Donald Trump and Chinese leader Xi Jinping in Washington last week.

The White House said that under a so-called "30-for-30" framework, each country would be allowed to import "non-sensitive" goods worth $30 billion from the other at reduced tariff rates.

The more favorable tariff treatment followed recommendations from the US-China Board of Trade and would improve market access for about 30% of US exports to China, US trade representative Jamieson Greer said in a statement Sunday.

"The Trump Administration will continue to pursue fair, balanced, and reciprocal trade with China by ensuring compliance with commitments on agricultural and energy purchases, pursuing balanced trade in non-sensitive goods, and securing market access for American farmers, manufacturers, businesses, and workers," he added.

The Chinese list of US products that will be subject to lower tariffs covers 1,619 items, including corn, wheat, frozen meat, seafood, wood products, cosmetics and medical devices, according to a list published by the White House . US soybeans were not included, a blow to struggling American farmers who have been collateral damage from a years-long tit-for-tat trade war between the two countries.

The White House also said that China would import at least 10 million metric tons of coal from the United States in 2027 and again in 2028. Previous commitments to import certain quantities of goods, such as agricultural products, have not always been met in full, however.

The US list of Chinese imports covers 77 items, including toys, tableware, kitchen accessories, curtains, electric shavers and inflatable balls.

The Chinese commerce ministry said the agreement would "further stabilize" China-US economic and trade relations and "create favorable conditions" for the export of relevant Chinese products to the United States.

The announcement comes after the US and China agreed ahead of Xi's visit to press pause on escalating tariff measures until January 10. The trade truce – which sets tariff levels at 30% on Chinese goods and 10% on US goods – has been extended multiple times since May 2025, when the two countries met in Geneva for negotiations.

articles.title: Nvidia says its new AI safety platform can contain rogue agents within ‘milliseconds’
articles.summary: Nvidia is launching a new AI safety platform designed to prevent rogue hacking incidents.
articles.body: Nvidia is launching a new safety platform designed to contain and monitor AI agents, a move that comes in response to a wave of rogue hacking incidents, as reported earlier by Reuters. In an announcement on Monday, Nvidia says its new Open Agent Safety Platform can quarantine agents that attempt to escape their boundaries within “milliseconds.” The platform uses Nvidia’s OpenShell open-source software, which runs on the company’s Vera AI CPU. Users can choose the information an AI agent can access, and OpenShell checks these restrictions before and during a task, according to Nvidia. It also includes Nvidia’s Sentry technology on a separate chip to continuously monitor agents and enforce boundaries. Concerns about AI safety have risen in recent weeks, as OpenAI, Anthropic, and Google have all revealed incidents where their AI models went outside their testing environments and hacked other companies. Several major tech companies are backing Nvidia’s Open Agent Safety Platform, including Anthropic, Microsoft, and SpaceX.

articles.title: FBI reportedly declares 'cyber security incident' after hackers steal agents' personal data | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The bureau has not yet publicly confirmed a breach, but has told its agents that their personal information and Social Security numbers were exposed.
articles.body:
The Federal Bureau of Investigation has reportedly told its agents and support staff that their personal information was stolen in a recent cyberattack that targeted the bureau’s job application portal.

It’s the bureau’s first acknowledgment that the personal information of FBI agents was taken in the breach. The FBI has not publicly confirmed a breach beyond a statement last week, in which it said it was aware that a hacking group had claimed a cyberattack but that the theft of data was “still undetermined.”

As reported by MS Now reporter Ken Dilanian over the weekend, the FBI has since declared a “cyber security incident” in an internal notification to staff, telling employees that their names, addresses, job titles, and their Social Security numbers were exposed.

Several media outlets have since confirmed that some of the stolen data included medical information, such as records relating to blood and urine samples , as well as psychiatric reports .

The hacking group called ShinyHunters previously told TechCrunch that they “have data on mostly all of FBI,” and a “substantial” amount of information on applicants who applied through the FBIJobs.gov portal. The hackers broke in by exploiting a vulnerability in an Oracle PeopleSoft server, which hosts reams of human resources information on agents and now-employees who applied through the portal.

The hackers told TechCrunch that they are not seeking a financial ransom but are demanding the correction of an earlier FBI-issued report, which they say misrepresents their activities.

Justin Sherman, a national security expert, called the data breach a “counterintelligence disaster” for the U.S. government in a blog post for Lawfare . He warned that the data theft would “expose thousands of FBI personnel to profiling, phishing, foreign intelligence approaches, and much more.”

While the bureau has notified employees, it’s less clear if the FBI has disclosed the incident to lawmakers in Congress who have oversight of the FBI. Under federal law , alerting Congress is required when an intrusion meets the bar of a “major incident” — such as if a data breach involves the theft of personally identifiable information that is “likely to result in demonstrable harm” to U.S. national security.

It’s likely that bureau lawyers are trying to figure that out right now. If a disclosure is required, it would be the FBI’s second known notification to lawmakers this year about a data breach, after hackers, suspected to be Chinese, broke into a surveillance system that exposed targets of FBI surveillance and investigations earlier this year.

A White House spokesperson deferred comment to the FBI when asked if the bureau had declared a major incident. A spokesperson for the FBI did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment on Monday. Representatives for several lawmakers whose jurisdictions cover oversight of the FBI did not have any immediate answers.

ABC News reports that the FBI’s job site has been the primary way to apply for a job with the bureau since 2017. The portal remains down at the time of publication.

articles.title: The next connected device could be the shirt you're wearing
articles.summary: ShareAScan turns T-shirts into scannable digital business cards with QR codes that link to profiles the owner can update anytime they choose.
articles.body: A T-shirt has always been able to tell you something about the person wearing it. Maybe it shows a favorite band, sports team or funny message. Now, it can potentially open an entire digital profile. That is the idea behind ShareAScan, a startup using QR code clothing to connect apparel and other physical products with digital content that can change over time. Scan a code with your smartphone and you can see whatever experience the owner has chosen to share. That might include text, photos, video, music, a portfolio, social content or information about a business. The shirt itself does not contain a battery, Bluetooth connection or hidden computer. The technology starts with a printed QR code and the web platform behind it. So, could the next connected device actually be something you wear? Missed CyberGuy LIVE? No technical experience is needed. Watch the free replay + downloadable checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com EMPTY ENVELOPES IN YOUR MAILBOX? DO NOT SCAN THAT CODE How QR code clothing works The basic idea is simple. ShareAScan prints a unique QR code on products such as T-shirts, hoodies, hats, mugs and other merchandise. A person scans the code using the camera already built into a smartphone. No special scanning app is required. However, the interesting part happens behind that code. Instead of permanently tying the printed QR code to one piece of content, ShareAScan lets the owner change what appears later. The physical code stays the same while the digital experience behind it changes. For example, someone could use a shirt to share a portfolio at a conference and later update the content to promote a project or event. The company describes its technology as a patent-pending platform connecting physical products with dynamic, user-controlled digital identities. Its September announcement says a single product can become a changing introduction, portfolio, personal message or business card. That makes the concept more interesting than simply printing a website address across your chest. The idea recently made its way to the Emmys ShareAScan was founded by sisters Shara and Kailey Zuckerman. Shara is a college student studying business, finance and artificial intelligence, while Kailey is still in high school. The company got a major dose of exposure this month when its QR merchandise was included in gift bags distributed around the 78th Emmy Awards. ShareAScan merchandise went into gift bags for nominees, presenters and performers. Still, the bigger story goes beyond an awards-show gift bag. It is another example of physical products gaining a digital layer that can change long after you buy them. Your shirt could become a changing digital business card There are plenty of ways people could use this. A business owner could wear a shirt that introduces a company. A creator could share recent work. Someone at a conference could use it as a digital introduction. Meanwhile, a musician could share new content or an organization could promote an event. Because the material behind the QR code can change, the same physical product can serve different purposes over time. ShareAScan says purchases start at $19 and current customers do not pay an ongoing subscription fee. The company also tells CyberGuy that customers who buy under the current model will not later face a subscription charge even if its terms change for future customers. That gives the physical product something most ordinary clothing never had before: content that can keep changing after you take it home. What happens when someone scans your shirt? ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that scans are anonymous. The company says it collects no information about the scanner unless an owner's access restrictions require it to check whether that scanner is allowed to view the content. If someone does not have permission, the company says that person simply does not receive access. ShareAScan also says it does not currently give the wearer scan analytics. In other words, wearing one of these products does not give you a dashboard showing who walked by and scanned your code. The company says owners can choose who gets access to their content and can completely delete their account and associated data. However, there is still another side to privacy: what you decide to reveal. If you make your full name, workplace, photos, social accounts or other personal information publicly available, someone who scans you may learn quite a bit. That is why anyone using connected clothing should look at the experience from a stranger's point of view before wearing it in public. QR CODE EMAIL SCAM TARGETS EMPLOYEE REVIEWS Can a ShareAScan QR code send you to a malicious website? This required an important clarification from the company. ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that its QR codes cannot point directly to an outside website. Instead, scanning the code first opens the experience hosted through its platform. However, content within that experience can include links. The company says it scans uploads for malicious links, phishing links, pornography and other inappropriate material. It also says people review flagged material. ShareAScan acknowledges that its screening cannot catch everything. That makes its setup different from a random QR sticker that directly sends your browser to an unknown website. Even so, you should never treat every QR code as automatically safe simply because scanning has become second nature. The FTC continues to warn about criminals using QR codes to send people to fake websites designed to steal passwords, financial information and other personal data. In a fresh warning published Sept. 3, the agency again advised people to inspect the destination before opening a QR link. So, the familiar security advice still applies whenever you pick up your phone to scan something. ShareAScan requires users to be 18 or older Connected clothing could naturally catch the attention of younger users, especially when it links fashion with social content. ShareAScan tells CyberGuy that account holders must be at least 18 years old. At the same time, the company acknowledges that an age requirement cannot completely stop someone younger from trying to create an account. That makes conversations about public sharing especially important for families. A QR code someone wears outside can potentially expose information to people they have never met. What happens after you wash the shirt? A scannable shirt also has to hold up to everyday wear. ShareAScan says its QR codes have been tested through repeated washing and continue to scan after normal use. Of course, a QR code still needs to remain physically readable. Heavy damage, fading or distortion could eventually interfere with any printed code. There is another longevity issue too. Unlike a normal graphic on a shirt, this feature depends on the online platform behind it. ShareAScan says it plans to keep the platform operating and has purchased insurance intended to help support continued operation. That is worth keeping in mind with any connected product that depends on a company's servers long after the initial purchase. QR codes are becoming part of the physical world QR codes are already everywhere, from tickets and restaurant tables to payment screens and packages. Now, they are starting to show up on the things we wear. ShareAScan takes that familiar technology and gives it a more personal use. Instead of linking to one fixed piece of information, the code can connect to content that the owner changes over time. That means a sweatshirt could introduce your business at a conference, while a T-shirt could share your latest project, interests or something you simply want people to know about you. A quick scan could even become an easy way to start a conversation. But once your clothing can share information about you, it is worth thinking about exactly what you are putting out there. Anything you make public could potentially be seen by someone you have never met. Look at exactly what appears to someone who does not know you. Avoid exposing your home address, private phone number, personal email or other sensitive information. 2) Use the privacy controls Review who can access your content. ShareAScan says owners can limit access, so use those controls when you want to share something with a smaller group. 3) Separate public and private information Create content specifically for public sharing. That can help you avoid giving strangers access to personal accounts filled with years of photos, posts or identifying information. 4) Think before opening anything after a scan Treat QR codes like links. ShareAScan says it screens content on its platform, but QR codes in general can still lead to trouble. If anything asks for a password, payment information or other sensitive data unexpectedly, stop. 5) Check the destination Look at the address your phone shows before opening a QR link. The FTC recommends checking for misspellings and switched letters that can signal an impersonation site. 6) Keep strong antivirus protection active Install and keep strong antivirus software active on your devices. Also, keep your phone's built-in security protections and software updates turned on too. No security tool can make every QR code safe, so always check where a code is taking you before entering passwords, payment information or other sensitive data. Kurt's key takeaways What I like about this idea is how simple it is. There is no battery, Bluetooth or complicated hardware inside the shirt. The QR code does the work, and the person wearing it can keep changing what people see after they scan. ShareAScan also says it has built in some useful controls. Scans are anonymous, owners can limit who sees their content and the code itself does not send you straight to an outside website. The company also says it checks uploaded content for malicious material. The bigger question is how much of yourself you want to make scannable. articles.title: Fed's Cook warns AI and oil prices will continue to push up inflation
articles.summary: Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook said Monday that she believes AI and higher oil prices will continue to push up inflation in the coming months.
articles.body:
Federal Reserve governor Lisa Cook said Monday that she believes AI and higher oil prices will continue to push up inflation in the coming months, but that any further interest rate hikes would be contingent on economic data.

"I expect to see continued pressure on inflation from the AI build-out … and from the pass-through of higher oil prices and supply chain disruptions associated with the conflict in the Middle East," Cook said in a speech in Oakland, California.

She noted that the job market appears well-positioned to handle an increase in rates.

Looking ahead, Cook said she will consider what policy rate may be needed to continue to guide inflation down to the Fed's target.

"The number and magnitude of any future adjustments will be informed by observations of the economy's reaction to our policy actions thus far and the inflation and labor data over the coming months," she said.

Cook warned that while AI is contributing to inflation in specific sectors right now, demand for the technology could ripple through the broader economy.

Cook pointed out that prices for AI-related goods — such as chips, computers, and software — have surged, reflecting the demand in those sectors, not economy-wide. She cautioned that trying to quell inflation in specific sectors stemming from AI with rate hikes would be a mistake.

"Attempting to fight sector-specific inflation with monetary policy could be a mistake," Cook said. "Our tools are too blunt to target narrow sectors, and addressing relative price shifts is not our role."

However, she said she does see some "economy-wide pressure" from AI-fueled demand, citing data center investments that rely on construction labor and energy and are widely used across many other sectors. As a result, increased AI investment could introduce price pressure to those other sectors. And with even more investment in the pipeline, she said, that could increase demand even further.

Signs in the inflation data suggest the pressure may be broadening, Cook added, pointing to electricity and water costs that have risen around 5% over the past year. She also noted core goods prices are running over 3% this year.

She also said a large portion of the rise in stock prices over the past few years can be attributed to enthusiasm about AI, and that added wealth appears to be feeding through to household spending.

"This introduces the risk that, even as inflation in the narrow AI sector moderates, new and more broadly based price pressures may take its place," Cook said.

articles.title: UK police to release 5 men arrested in US air base incident
articles.summary: The five men arrested in connection with a possible terrorist attack at a British air base operated by the U.S. military have been released on bail but remain under investigation, according to the United Kingdom’s counterterrorism police. All five men — who are British nationals from London and are between 23 and 25 years old…
articles.body:
The five men arrested in connection with a possible terrorist attack at a British air base operated by the U.S. military have been released on bail but remain under investigation, according to the United Kingdom’s counterterrorism police.

All five men — who are British nationals from London and are between 23 and 25 years old — were arrested Sunday on explosives and terror charges near the Royal Air Force (RAF) Fairford air base in southern England after three vans were seen outside the military installation.

Laurence Taylor, the head of Britain’s counterterrorism police, later told reporters the men’s release would be “subject to stringent conditions on their movement and contact with others.”

He noted that detectives were investigating the incident “from every possible angle, including that this may be actively committed by proxies or individuals, either knowingly or unknowingly, working on behalf of a foreign state.”

Taylor did not say whether investigators had found explosives in any of the three vans and did not take questions.

His statement added to the confusion around the incident, which began after a farmer alerted police to three suspicious vehicles near the air base at 12:45 a.m. local time Sunday.

A local farmer reportedly said she called police after seeing the vans and came across “a large group of men,” some with their faces covered, as she drove home late Saturday night. She said the men ran away when they saw her vehicle.

Members from the British army’s explosive ordnance disposal team used a robot to examine the vans, though it’s unclear what, if anything, was found.

President Trump later on Sunday contradicted British police when he told reporters the suspects had been “under view for a long time” and intended to do “big damage” to the air base.

Iran has denied its involvement in the event, with its London Embassy saying it “categorically rejects and strongly condemns the recent unfounded and malicious speculations” around the incident.

The U.S. has used RAF Fairford to position B-52 and B-1 bombers for missions to Iran since the U.S. and Israel’s joint war began in February.

Tehran has repeatedly threatened countries that aid Washington in the war and has already been linked to a series of attacks in Europe, heightening tensions across the continent.

articles.title: US aircraft carrier deploys to Middle East to relieve USS George Washington
articles.summary: The USS Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, is headed for the Middle East to relieve another carrier already in theater as tensions with Iran persist. The USS Theodore Roosevelt, the flagship vessel of Carrier Strike Group 9, left San Diego on Sunday, according to ship-watcher WarshipCam. The carrier will provide a substitute for Japan-based…
articles.body:
The USS Theodore Roosevelt, a Nimitz-class aircraft carrier, is headed for the Middle East to relieve another carrier already in theater as tensions with Iran persist.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt, the flagship vessel of Carrier Strike Group 9, left San Diego on Sunday, according to ship-watcher WarshipCam . The carrier will provide a substitute for Japan-based USS George Washington, which was dispatched to the U.S. Central Command (Centcom) region last month.

The U.S. Navy did not immediately respond to The Hill’s request for comment.

The Roosevelt’s deployment comes as the U.S. has worked to boost the flow of oil through the Strait of Hormuz and as U.S. warships continue to enforce the naval blockade in the Arabian Sea.

Since July, U.S. forces have redirected 122 commercial vessels to ensure compliance with the effort, Centcom said in an update Friday .

U.S. military officials have said that more than 1 billion barrels of oil have passed through the key waterway over the past few months.

The U.S. has had at least one aircraft carrier in the Centcom region since President Trump kick-started the U.S. war with Iran in late February. The other aircraft carrier operating in the Middle East is the USS George H.W. Bush.

The USS George Washington was sent to the Middle East to replace the USS Abraham Lincoln, whose deployment has come under fire from Democratic lawmakers and sailors’ family members following reports of rough onboard conditions and worsening mental health.

“We’ve been in conflict pretty much the whole time I’ve been in the seat, and that’s certainly stressed the force,” Chief of Naval Operations Adm. Daryl Caudle told reporters last month. “I’m trying to work with my chain of command to put the extension process in a way that gives more certainty for planning.”

He added later, “If we know we’re going into harm’s way, we should be able to project with a little bit more fidelity how long the carrier and the strike group is going to stay on station.”

“We do these extensions in little chunks, and the families don’t see any endpoint so they can plan their own lives,” Caudle continued. “That creates a lot of stress for sailors.”

Eisenhower in the Navy’s campaign against attacks by Yemen’s Houthi rebels targeting shipping in the Red Sea corridor over the Israel-Hamas war in the Gaza Strip.

articles.title: Nvidia boosts buyback plan by $150B in new record
articles.summary: Technology giant Nvidia announced Monday it is boosting its stock buyback program by $150 billion, setting a record for the largest repurchasing allotment in history. The company’s board of directors authorized the increase, which boosts the total amount in Nvidia’s buyback program from $85 billion to $235 billion. Apple authorized a $110 billion buyback program…
articles.body:
Technology giant Nvidia announced Monday it is boosting its stock buyback program by $150 billion, setting a record for the largest repurchasing allotment in history.

The company’s board of directors authorized the increase , which boosts the total amount in Nvidia’s buyback program from $85 billion to $235 billion. Apple authorized a $110 billion buyback program in 2024, which was a record at the time.

Growing demand for chips to power AI data centers has sent Nvidia’s profits soaring, as the company last month reported $96.2 billion in revenue for the second quarter of this year. That marked an increase of 106 percent relative to the second quarter of 2025.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said Monday the company’s growth “is being driven by a once-in-a-generation platform shift to AI and accelerated computing.”

Huang added in a release , “Our cash generation gives us the capacity to invest in the technologies that advance this transformation and return capital to shareholders. This authorization reflects our confidence in the long-term opportunity ahead.”

The company’s stock jumped Monday after the company’s announcement, and it was up by roughly 2.1 percent, to nearly $230 per share, as of mid-afternoon. At the start of the year, the tech giant’s stock was trading at about $190 per share.

Nvidia reported $89 billion in revenue from data centers alone last quarter, up 117 percent from the second quarter of 2025. The company projected $108 billion — plus or minus 2 percent — in revenue for the third quarter.

The firm has also reached a deal to acquire open-source platform Hugging Face for $12.93 billion , which will give it access to more than 3 million models and 500,000 datasets used by thousands of companies.

In July, OpenAI agents went rogue and hacked into Hugging Face’s systems without any prompt to do so.

Also on Monday, Nvidia unveiled a new platform that it says will put guardrails on AI agents at the software and hardware level. Organizations can tailor their use of the platform based on their requirements, the company noted in a release .

“To date, model safety has been about training good behavior into the model,” said Justin Boitano, vice president of enterprise AI at Nvidia, on a call Sunday.

“The industry calls that model alignment,” he continued. “For probabilistic systems, this approach has obvious limitations. That’s why we’re introducing a deterministic system to mediate and enforce how these agents behave.”

Huang, who attended a state dinner President Trump hosted on Thursday in honor of Chinese President Xi Jinping, has argued AI companies do not need antitrust exemptions to coordinate a slowdown in model development.

While the Nvidia CEO said earlier this month AI safety “is a real thing,” he did not express concern about technology posing an imminent threat to humanity.

“We’re not going to die in 2030,” Huang told host Jim Cramer on CNBC’s “ Mad Money .”

“There are so many people in the world who are going to build AI properly,” he added. “We’re going to have all kinds of guardrails, invent all kinds of technology for safety and security.”

Julia Shapero and Miranda Nazzaro contributed.

articles.title: Trump Denies Asking China’s Xi About Potential US Arms Sales
articles.summary: President Donald Trump said he has not discussed selling arms to China, contradicting a suggestion made by his ambassador to Beijing.
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- President Donald Trump said he has not discussed selling arms to China, contradicting a suggestion made by his ambassador to Beijing.

"I never heard of that," the president told reporters in the Oval Office on Monday, when asked about Ambassador David Perdue's statement over the weekend. Trump initially appeared confused and clarified if the reporter meant arms sales to Taiwan.

Perdue told Fox News on Sunday that Trump had asked Chinese President Xi Jinping if he would to like to buy some American armaments.

"They probably like to buy it because we do make better equipment than that. So maybe it's a good idea. But we didn't discuss that," Trump said on Monday.

Any suggestion that the US would sell arms to China would send shockwaves through the US national security community and alarm Washington's allies, given that Beijing is the US's chief geopolitical rival.

articles.title: US says GM tech costs to drop by $20 billion through 2031 due to new emissions rules
articles.summary: (Refiles to spell out "billion" in headline) By David Shepardson WASHINGTON, Sept 28 (Reuters) - General Motors will see its technology costs decline by $20....
articles.body:
(Refiles to spell out "billion" in headline)

WASHINGTON, Sept 28 (Reuters) - General Motors will see its technology costs decline by $20.4 billion through ‌2031 as a result of drastically lower vehicle fuel economy rules ‌finalized Monday, the US Transportation Department said.

In total, the Trump administration estimates automakers' technology costs will ​decline by $60.6 billion through 2031, or about $1,289 per vehicle, as a result. The 2024 fuel economy rules had been estimated to cost GM $31.7 billion through 2031.

The new rule is expected to take effect around early December. Automakers will not need to ‌add expensive emissions equipment ⁠to reduce fuel consumption or build more EVs, as they would have had to under the prior rule in order to ⁠meet more stringent requirements.

The department's National Highway Traffic Safety Administration (NHTSA) said Chrysler-parent Stellantis's costs will decline by $6.6 billion, Ford by $5.8 billion, Toyota by $4.5 billion and Honda by $4.1 ​billion.

GM said ​it supports the goals of the ​rule and its "intention to better align ‌fuel economy standards with market realities."

Last year, Congress passed legislation ending penalties for not meeting fuel economy requirements after Stellantis paid about $775 million in civil penalties for failing to meet US fuel economy requirements since 2019.

GM paid $128.2 million in penalties for 2016 and 2017. GM also paid a $145.8 million penalty and ‌forfeited fuel economy credits worth hundreds of millions ​of dollars at the time after a government ​investigation found excess emissions from ​approximately 5.9 million GM vehicles.

In 2023, under former President Joe ‌Biden, NHTSA said its proposal to ​hike fuel economy standards ​through 2032 would cost the industry $14 billion in projected fines including $6.5 billion for GM, $3 billion for Stellantis and $1 billion for Ford Motor.

The final ​rule adopted in 2024 ‌eased requirements and said the auto industry would face no more than $1.83 ​billion in fines from 2027 through 2031.

articles.title: GOP Leader Thune Says Taxpayers Shouldn’t Pay for Trump TV Ads
articles.summary: Senate Republican Leader John Thune said taxpayers shouldn’t be footing the bill for video advertisements lauding President Donald Trump that the administrat...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- Senate Republican Leader John Thune said taxpayers shouldn't be footing the bill for video advertisements lauding President Donald Trump that the administration has called "presidential public service announcements."

One television advertisement airing on cable and broadcast networks praises Trump with a photo montage while another features outtakes from a Trump speech and a voiceover by the president saying that a US "golden age" has begun.

The ads aired on national television over the weekend, including on Sunday morning public affairs shows and several college and NFL football games.

"It's a great message, I like the message, but it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer dollars," Thune told reporters at the Capitol on Monday.

Democrats and the watchdog group Public Citizen have called the government funding for the ads illegal. Such advertisements would typically be paid for by political committees separate from the government.

Thune's criticism is the latest public break by the Senate majority leader, who has until recently largely avoided public criticism of the president. Republicans face unusually strong competition to retain US Senate seats in typically stalwart GOP states such as Kansas, Nebraska, Iowa, Alaska and Texas.

The White House defended public funding for the video ads in a statement, saying that Trump "is not on the ballot" in the midterms and they are "a reminder for Americans to love their country."

Democrats counter that the ads violate language in this year's government spending law that prohibits the use of funds "for publicity or propaganda purposes within the United States not heretofore authorized by Congress." They also say it violates the Hatch Act, which prevents public servants from acting on behalf of political campaigns.

articles.summary: An Arizona-based tour company is suing the Trump administration over its move to impose higher national park visitor fees on people who don’t live in the U.S. In a new filing Monday, Across Arizona Tours said it has lost business because of the higher costs for nonresidents imposed by the administration earlier this year. articles.body:
An Arizona-based tour company is suing the Trump administration over its move to impose higher national park visitor fees on people who don’t live in the U.S.

In a new filing Monday , Across Arizona Tours said it has lost business because of the higher costs for nonresidents imposed by the administration earlier this year.

The company’s Carole Stapleton spoke with 80-90 potential customers who did not book a tour with the firm, often citing the higher fees, according to the lawsuit.

The case, in which the company is represented by the libertarian-leaning Pacific Legal Foundation, argues that the policy goes beyond the administration’s statutory authority.

“Federal agencies cannot make up fees as they please,” Jacob Haas, an attorney with Pacific Legal Foundation, said in a written statement. “Only Congress can authorize federal fees. And Congress has never authorized higher fees for nonresidents — not least because such a policy would discourage international tourism and hurt companies like Across Arizona Tours.”

The Trump administration has imposed fees of an additional $100 per person at some of the nation’s most-visited national parks for those who don’t live in the U.S. Nonresidents who buy annual passes also have to pay more — $250, compared with $80 for residents — under the policy .

An Interior Department spokesperson argued that U.S. residents already subsidize national parks by paying taxes.

“Thanks to President Donald J. Trump, U.S. residents, who already fund the National Park System through federal taxes, are continuing to enjoy affordable pricing, while foreign tourists are paying higher entrance fees to help maintain our parks and improve visitor experiences,” said the spokesperson, who did not provide their name and replied from a generic press email account.

“This administration will continue to put American families first — making parks more accessible, more affordable and more efficient for future generations,” the spokesperson added.

articles.summary: A group of news outlets suing OpenAI for copyright infringement argued Monday that the court should give “little weight” to the views of the Department of Justice (DOJ), which signaled support for the AI firm earlier this month. The New York Times, Chicago Tribune and other outlets in the case suggested the administration “may have…
articles.body:
A group of news outlets suing OpenAI for copyright infringement argued Monday that the court should give “little weight” to the views of the Department of Justice (DOJ), which signaled support for the AI firm earlier this month.

The New York Times, Chicago Tribune and other outlets in the case suggested the administration “may have been influenced by extraneous considerations—up to and including the Administration’s political and financial interests.”

They pointed to the relationship between the Trump administration and AI companies, including donations.

“Although one could argue that political factors will always influence Government litigation positions to some extent, the nature, extent, and transparency of the AI industry’s efforts to influence this Administration should not be lightly dismissed,” the outlets added.

The Times initially sued OpenAI in 2023, accusing the company of improperly training AI models on the newspaper’s copyrighted content. It has since been joined by several other outlets.

OpenAI argues its actions fall under the “fair use” doctrine, which allows for the use of some copyrighted content without permission.

The Trump administration backed the company in a filing in early September, suggesting the news outlets’ interpretation of fair use “would thwart such creative and scientific progress while hindering American prosperity and economic mobility.”

The outlets underscored Monday that the government usually consults with the relevant government agencies before offering a statement of interest in a case. But Axios reported earlier this month that the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office and Copyright Office were taken by surprise.

“[T]he DOJ not only failed to consider the Copyright Office’s position—it attempts to undermine the Office’s position by accusing the Office of ‘threadbare reasoning’ and noting the Administration’s efforts to remove the Register of Copyrights,” the outlets added.

New York Times spokesperson Graham James said in a statement that the government’s filing “appears to be an effort to further enrich the world’s largest companies—and the Administration’s largest donors—while undermining this country’s free press.”

“Time and time again the American economy has shown that copyright protections aren’t at odds with innovation, but rather fuel it,” he added.

The video, which was posted Sunday on a DHS social media account, responded to a headline…
articles.body:
The Department of Homeland Security (DHS) is refusing a request from the NFL and former Philadelphia Eagles player Brian Dawkins to take down a video it posted using the Hall of Fame safety to promote President Trump’s immigration agenda .

The video, which was posted Sunday on a DHS social media account, responded to a headline that claimed, “Huge migrant caravan headed towards the US southern border.”

“Our time has come,” the department wrote, attaching a clip of Dawkins making violent tackles and pumping up fans and teammates.

The NFL asked the DHS on Monday to take the video down, The Athletic first reported .

“DHS is playing lockdown defense at the border. We will use every Weapon at our disposal, from A to X, to keep Americans safe,” a spokesperson for the department told The Hill in response to the NFL’s request.

In a video posted on his own social media account, Dawkins said he did not give permission for his name, image and likeness “to be used by anybody.”

“Take a deep breath,” he said. “Ya’ll be blessed.”

During his more than decade in the NFL, Dawkins was one of the most feared safeties in the league and was known for punishing hits and game-saving tackles.

Trump and his allies have increasingly used sports imagery to attempt to connect with voters, with the president attending the University of Texas vs. University of Tennessee football game Saturday before pro golf’s president’s cup Sunday.

articles.title: Hegseth instructs Pentagon to defend 2026 elections from ‘foreign actors’
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth instructed the Pentagon last week to prioritize and deploy “advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities” to track down, disrupt and neutralize “foreign actors to protect the 2026 midterm elections” while “maintaining the fundamental freedoms that characterize our country.” “Commander U.S. Cyber Command and the Directors of the Combat Support Agencies will prioritize…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth instructed the Pentagon last week to prioritize and deploy “advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities” to track down, disrupt and neutralize “foreign actors to protect the 2026 midterm elections” while “maintaining the fundamental freedoms that characterize our country.”

“Commander U.S. Cyber Command and the Directors of the Combat Support Agencies will prioritize the use of DoW [Department of War] intelligence and cyber capabilities to ensure foreign actors do not meddle in our democratic systems,” Hegseth said in a Sept. 22 memo , which was made public Monday.

The Pentagon chief directed the Defense Intelligence Enterprise to execute collection and production on foreign threats to U.S. elections in accordance with the “law, regulation, Executive direction and DoW policies and directives.”

Hegseth instructed Gen. Joshua Rudd, head of U.S. Cyber Command, to use existing capabilities and authorities in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security to counter “potential cyber threats from foreign actors targeting our elections.”

“Our Nation’s ability to conduct free and fair elections is a steadfast principal of our Democracy,” Hegseth said in the one-page memo. “Assuring and protecting this ability is a no-fail mission and the DoW will do its part in supporting this whole of government effort.”

The meddling of foreign actors and nations has been a concern for U.S. administrations.

Similarly, in 2022, the National Security Agency (NSA) and U.S. Cyber Command under former President Biden highlighted a similar push to safeguard the 2022 midterms from foreign interference and influence.

Rudd told senators during a hearing in January that he would work on safeguarding U.S. elections and protect from foreign interference.

“U.S. Cyber Command and the National Security Agency are closely partnered to identify and defend against cyber threats to our nation. The Command and the Agency regularly counter actions by malicious foreign cyber actors including those with the intent to interfere with our democratic process,” Rudd said in a statement Monday.

articles.title: Scott Bessent Says Kevin Warsh Is 'Well Aware' of AI Productivity Gains: Fed Should Keep an 'Open Mind' on Interest Rates

articles.body:

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Sunday that the Federal Reserve, under chair Kevin Warsh , should keep "an open mind" as growth accelerates, citing artificial intelligence-driven productivity and the administration's deregulation push as reasons inflation can remain contained.

Speaking with Larry Kudlow on Fox News' Sunday Morning Futures, Bessent said that during former Fed chair Alan Greenspan's era, the Fed "let things run" because of productivity gains tied to the internet, while today's gains are "probably the same kind of gains, if not more substantial now."

He said the Fed "should have an open mind because… we have created supply with deregulation."

The Treasury Secretary argued that deregulation has expanded supply fast enough to absorb a private-sector demand shock, unlike the regulatory constriction he blamed for inflation under former President Joe Biden .

Bessent added that Warsh, President Donald Trump 's choice for Fed chair, was "well aware" of the productivity gains.

"Core inflation has been very quiescent," Bessent said, adding that it has dropped in recent months, blaming elevated headline inflation on oil prices driven up by the war in Iran.

In August, headline consumer price inflation rose 3.4% year over year, while core inflation slowed to 2.4%, and energy prices jumped 16.3%.

Bessent predicted oil would fall once the conflict was resolved, pulling headline inflation back toward core.

Earlier this month, Trump said oil prices will fall "precipitously" once the U.S. wins its war with Iran, predicting gas will first drop to $3 a gallon before ultimately falling below $2.

The Federal Reserve raised its benchmark interest rate by 25 basis points to a range of 3.75%-4.00%, marking the first rate hike since 2023.

articles.title: Grandmother sues after alleged AI facial recognition error led to months in jail, experts sound alarm
articles.summary: Angela Lipps was arrested at gunpoint and jailed for nearly six months after Fargo police allegedly relied on an uncorroborated AI facial recognition match.
articles.body: A Tennessee grandmother has filed a lawsuit against a North Dakota city and police department, accusing officials of wrongfully detaining her for nearly six months after allegedly misusing artificial intelligence facial recognition technology to investigate a bank theft case. Angela Lipps, now 50, of Elizabethton, Tennessee, said she was caring for her neighbor's four young children when police showed up at the home and arrested her at gunpoint in July 2025. The complaint, filed Sept. 15, 2026, alleges that authorities relied exclusively on a flawed AI facial recognition match to extradite Lipps from Tennessee to North Dakota, despite her having no connection to the crime or the state. Experts on police technology told Fox News Digital that the case is among more than a dozen known instances involving alleged police mishandling of facial recognition technology. "I sat in a county jail in Tennessee for 108 days," Lipps said in a GoFundMe post. "They said I was fugitive from justice. I had no bail. No one interviewed me. I just sat and waited." FRAUD EXPERT WARNS AI IS HELPING CRIMINALS OUTPACE THE GOVERNMENT: 'DON'T HAVE THE RIGHT TOOLS' The bank theft case stemmed from April and May 2025, when an unknown woman allegedly used fake IDs and stolen identities to perpetrate bank fraud in Fargo and West Fargo, North Dakota, according to the lawsuit. Officials then used a photo from a fraudulent ID card presented by the suspect, rather than surveillance footage, to conduct facial recognition searches using Clearview AI, prosecutors alleged. While Clearview AI explicitly requires facial recognition matches to be treated as potential leads, Fargo police allegedly characterized the AI match as a positive identification without disclosing that it had not been independently corroborated, according to the complaint. Meanwhile, the West Fargo Police Department reportedly declined to seek charges because the AI match was uncorroborated. A West Fargo police captain reportedly characterized AI facial recognition as "close to a last-ditch effort" in police investigations, the lawsuit said. FLOCK SAFETY CAMERAS NEED CONSTITUTIONAL GUARDRAILS BEFORE FURTHER DEPLOYMENT, TENNESSEE MAYOR ARGUES According to the complaint, Detective Lucas Heck did not review Lipps’ financial or travel records that showed she was in Tennessee during the bank thefts and failed to conduct photo lineups with bank tellers. Surveillance video reportedly showed physical differences between Lipps and the suspect, including a different build and a neck tattoo on Lipps that was absent from the suspect. "Heck ignored, concealed, and misrepresented exculpatory evidence that Lipps did not commit the bank thefts," the complaint alleged. On July 14, 2025, U.S. Marshals surrounded a neighbor’s house in Tennessee and arrested Lipps at gunpoint on a nationwide warrant, prosecutors said. Lipps was extradited to North Dakota and reportedly held on a $100,000 bond while facing eight felony counts, the most severe of which carried maximum sentences of up to 10 years in prison. Prosecutors dismissed all charges on Dec. 24, 2025, after Lipps produced bank records showing that she was in Tennessee when the bank thefts occurred, prosecutors said. "When she was released, she found that her residence, car, and personal property were lost while she was absent," the complaint said. FLOCK SAFETY CEO CALLS FOR NATIONAL 'COMPROMISE' AMID CAMERA SABOTAGE AND PUBLIC REVOLT Following public scrutiny, the Fargo Police Department and city of Fargo acknowledged at a March 2026 press conference that the department had made investigative errors. "When chief found some errors that were made in this area of where we got our facial recognition and how that worked, we immediately addressed it," Mayor Tim Mahoney said. Clare Garvie, the deputy director of Technology Law & Policy with the Policing Project, told Fox News Digital that incidents involving the alleged mishandling of AI have increased as law enforcement agencies adjust to "integrate AI and additional tools into police investigations." "We are aware of 16 misidentifications stemming from a face recognition match where someone was wrongfully arrested and spent time in jail because of that misidentification, and in many of these cases, it was because additional investigative steps weren't taken to prove, or in these cases to disprove, the face recognition match," Garvie said in an interview. "We're asking officers to do a different job now, such that we need to update how we think about these workflows," she added. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP In an interview with Fox News Digital, Nate Freed-Wessler, a deputy director at the American Civil Liberties Union, said the rise of artificial intelligence in law enforcement has fueled wrongful arrests across the country. "We've been seeing these kinds of wrongful arrests happening for at least five or six years now out of this kind of AI technology. And the rate of them seems to be increasing," he said. "We've seen cases where police intentionally avoid making any notes about their use of facial recognition technology or other AI."

articles.title: Pope Leo says AI concerns are not ‘fake news,’ must act on safety issues
articles.summary: Pope Leo XIV on Monday said mounting concerns about artificial intelligence software going rogue require discussions on how to regulate it, dismissing the notion that they are “fake news.” “If someone were to ask me, ‘Am I in panic mode?’ No, I’m not,” Leo told reporters while leaving France for Vatican City. “I sleep at…
articles.body:
Pope Leo XIV on Monday said mounting concerns about artificial intelligence software going rogue require discussions on how to regulate it, dismissing the notion that they are “fake news.”

“If someone were to ask me, ‘Am I in panic mode?’ No, I’m not,” Leo told reporters while leaving France for Vatican City. “I sleep at night. I do think that the concerns raised by many of the experts, specialists in AI should be taken seriously.”

The American pontiff added, “I don’t think that that is ‘fake news’ as some have said to try and cause whether financial or other some other kind of benefit,” noting that the world cannot “just sit back and pretend nothing is going to happen.”

Leo said days after the conclave elected him pope that AI presents one of the biggest challenges facing humanity.

“We need to continue to invite political leaders, leaders of AI, social organizations, associations to come together and look at what is happening already and what could be down the road,” he told reporters Monday. “To simply say, ‘Oh it’s not going to happen,’ and close our eyes to it, I think is probably not the most responsible way to go about that.”

Leo said he has received comments from people interested in joining the broader discussion on AI after he published his encyclical in May. The pope said he remains “relatively optimistic” that discussions will lead to solutions.

“I think there are enough people seriously interested in that and willing to look at that outside of the questions once again of power, who gets there first,” Leo said.

The discourse over AI has grown in recent weeks after several attempted and successful hacks committed by rogue AI software, including an attempted hack by OpenAI technology through the Department of Education website and improper interaction with the Securities and Exchange Commission and Census Bureau.

Members of Congress have called for stronger restrictions on AI, particularly after former Anthropic and OpenAI researcher Jacob Coxon suggested that AI could end human life by the end of the decade.

Some lawmakers have said that tech companies should pause while Congress gets to work on possible legislation to regulate AI. Others, like Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-Vt.) and Rep. Greg Casar (D-Texas), have called for a permanent ban on the development and deployment of artificial superintelligence.

President Trump has dismissed all concerns over the risks posed by AI. He cast warnings aside as a hoax but said he will launch an “AI Force” and an “AI czar” to oversee the technology’s development.

He told the United Nations General Assembly last Tuesday that official U.S. documents will refer to AI as “ super intelligence ,” saying that artificial makes the technology sound fake when it is “actually amazing.”

articles.title: Trump just banned Canadian booze — but there’s a big catch
articles.summary: President Donald Trump’s ban on Canadian booze kicked in on Tuesday, an unprecedented move that underscores the breakdown in one of the closest trading relat...
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's ban on Canadian booze kicked in on Tuesday, an unprecedented move that underscores the breakdown in one of the closest trading relationships in the world.

The ban, which impacts $800 million worth of Canadian alcoholic beverages the US imported last year, marks the latest salvo in a tit-for-tat trading war that already includes sky-high tariffs and a ban on US booze in Ontario and other Canadian provinces.

However, experts say most American shoppers are unlikely to immediately notice the ban, in part because of workarounds, exemptions and the fact that distributors have had time to stock up on imported Canadian alcohol before the ban took effect.

At the same time, with the quickly evolving trade picture with Canada, anything can change on a moment's notice. Hours before the ban took effect, Trump said he is confident the US will come out ahead, and expects Canada to come to the US with a deal soon.

"They want to have a deal with us, they call us all the time. The problem is that they've treated the United States very unfairly," Trump told reporters on Monday.

"Over the next three or four weeks, they're going to come to us and they're going to say, 'We're going to get rid of all the tariffs,'" Trump said. Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney has not said anything to that effect , however.

Whisky and liqueurs, two of Canada's top alcoholic beverage exports to the US, are exempt from the ban when sold in containers larger than four liters. In those cases, they also won't face any tariffs.

But making that switch requires having the right containers on hand or sourcing them from scratch, then rebottling smaller sizes more commonly sold in liquor stores. All that could add to businesses' costs – and potentially get tacked on to the prices consumers pay.

Crown Royal appears to be especially well-positioned since the company already sends bulk shipments of whisky to the United States, where it bottles all products sold domestically.

Beyond bulk exemptions, very few alcoholic beverages shipped from Canada were spared.

"Using import bans against an ally is unprecedented and a major deviation from US trade policy," said Inu Manak, a senior fellow focused on trade policy at the Peterson Institute for International Economics. "This is a very symbolic thing to target. It sends a message and is another form of escalation aimed at getting Canadian negotiators back to the table. But Prime Minister Carney is not in a rush to get a deal before the (US) midterms."
