articles.title: Your car’s data privacy problems are worse than you think
articles.summary: A new study found that nearly every automaker is transmitting data to third-party companies, including ones specializing in advertising and tracking.
articles.body: You hear it all the time: Modern cars are basically smartphones on wheels. And just like the phone in your pocket, the car in your driveway collects vast amounts of data — tracking where you drive, how fast you accelerate, how hard you brake, how aggressively you turn, and much more. The legality of this data harvesting remains hotly debated. Last year, the Federal Trade Commission penalized General Motors for illegally collecting and selling precise location and driving behavior data without informed consent. Other automakers, like Ford and Honda, have faced minor fines for making it overly difficult for customers to opt out. While industry observers long suspected that other carmakers were doing the same, the practice hadn’t been systematically investigated — until now. This week, researchers from Northeastern University, in collaboration with Consumer Reports, published an in-depth examination of connected vehicle privacy behaviors. Utilizing nearly two dozen vehicles from CR’s test fleet, the team sought to answer critical questions: Which cars transmit data? Who receives it? Does it cross international borders? And what personally identifiable information is actually being exposed? David Choffnes, project lead and former director of Northeastern’s Cybersecurity and Privacy Institute, said the goal was to reveal the sheer scale of modern vehicle data tracking and highlight how little visibility or control owners truly have over it. “I think the conclusion is that there’s a lot to be worried about,” Choffnes said in an interview. To get a complete picture, researchers analyzed 21 late-model vehicles from 19 brands currently sold in the US, along with 30 companion mobile apps linked to active vehicles. "“I think the conclusion is that there’s a lot to be worried about.”" - David Choffnes For traffic sent directly from the cars, the team identified the destination domains — including various third-party tracking companies — though they could not decrypt the encrypted payload data without hacking the vehicles. Intercepting Wi-Fi traffic proved relatively straightforward. Researchers placed a Raspberry Pi inside each car, connecting it to the vehicle’s Wi-Fi while routing its internet through a mobile hotspot. This setup let them monitor outgoing Wi-Fi traffic while the car was in motion. Capturing cellular traffic required a more creative approach. To avoid deploying an unauthorized cellular base station that could interfere with public networks, the team built a car-sized Faraday tent. The tent blocked all signal transmissions between the vehicle and external cell towers, forcing the car to fall back on the controlled Wi-Fi connection. The results were stark: Every single one of the 21 vehicles transmitted data to at least one third-party domain over Wi-Fi. Over half contacted domains specializing in advertising, tracking, or analytics (ATA). These companies, like Adobe, LexisNexis, and Amplitude, gather details about your vehicle or driving behavior to sell to insurance companies or target you with ads. Vehicles equipped with advanced infotainment systems — particularly those running Google’s Android Automotive OS with Google Automotive Services — contacted the highest number of third-party domains. Choffnes noted that an automaker’s choice of software platform directly impacts how much data reaches third parties. Google’s platform, for instance, includes built-in routines to communicate both with Google’s own services and external entities. “A lot of the tracking we also see through the apps that are built into the car,” Choffnes said. “So now, cars are essentially turning into the global smartphones.” Mobile apps present an equally insecure vector. The team discovered that seven companion apps — HondaLink, Lincoln, MyNissan, myCadillac, myChevrolet, myBuick, and myGMC — transmitted sensitive details like vehicle identification numbers (VINs), phone numbers, and precise locations directly to advertising networks. Over 70 percent of the tested companion apps contacted at least five unique ATA domains. Researchers were particularly alarmed by the pairing of a vehicle’s VIN with identifiable personal data, which allows data brokers to build detailed dossiers on individual drivers. “We sort of think, ‘Oh, well, if your online companies can track what you’re doing online, but you’re in your car, are they tracking what car you have?’” Choffnes said. “And so we’re seeing they actually can. And these are going to companies that probably most consumers don’t have a relationship with or have never heard of.” Automakers offered mixed reactions to the findings. Some defended their practices as legally compliant, while others acknowledged the vulnerabilities and issued software fixes. Honda, for example, requested that its analytics provider Amplitude delete all collected location data and updated the HondaLink app to cease transmitting geolocation after being presented with the Northeastern team’s findings. Choffnes believes the deeper issue is that consumers rarely understand what they agree to when buying a connected car or setting up its app. Most drivers will not sit in a dealership parking lot reading dense privacy policies on a tiny dashboard screen before agreeing to the terms. “I don’t think there’s a lot of trust as a result of this,” Choffnes said. “I think automakers would do well to earn that trust back. And one way to do that is through better transparency and helping consumers to not have data collected about them after they’ve made a really expensive purchase without having more explicit opt-in as opposed to opt-out.”

articles.title: Protego Ventures closes debut $125 million fund for Israeli defense tech | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Protego Ventures, the first and largest dedicated defense tech VC in Israel, just completed its final $125 million closing, TechCrunch learned exclusively.
articles.body:
Defense and venture capital used to rarely overlap, but that’s no longer the case. Defense tech VC dealmaking set a record in Q1 2026 , and new VC firms have emerged around the world to invest solely in defense startups.

One of these is two-year-old Protego Ventures , which presents itself as the first and largest dedicated defense tech VC in Israel. Led notably by two women, Lital Leshem and Lee Moser, it has just completed the final close of its debut fund with $125 million in capital commitments, TechCrunch learned exclusively.

This fund size is enabling Protego to invest between $5 million and $15 million per company, with a focus on startups “addressing the critical defense and security needs of Israel and the global community,” according to its website.

These include the likes of drone maker XTEND, its first portfolio company, which went public on the NYSE earlier this month. That’s also why Protego stopped short of its $150 million target: a smaller fund magnifies the impact of a single big win on overall returns, and with XTEND now looking like a potential “fund maker” — a single investment capable of returning the whole fund — raising more capital would only dilute that upside among a larger pool of investors. “Nobody wants to share the pie,” Leshem said.

Ares Management is one of Protego’s biggest backers. The investment firm suggested that Leshem and Moser join forces and start Protego in the aftermath of the October 7, 2023, Hamas attack on Israel, with the conviction that new technologies would be key to boosting Israel’s defense capabilities in the face of new threats, Leshem said.

With a $30 million investment as a limited partner, Ares gave Protego the support it needed to start investing right away, Leshem said. Besides XTEND, its portfolio also includes startups such as ASIO, which develops situational awareness systems and has partnered with Anduril .

Leshem says the reception in defense circles has been strong. “On the military side, there is a lot of respect, and people are coming — even under the radar — to talk to us, to learn from us, to train with us, and for sure get our technology and innovation.”

Still, the Israeli market is easier to navigate for insiders, and Protego’s two founders are leaning into their networks. Moser, a seasoned venture capitalist, will remain a managing partner at the generalist VC firm AnD Ventures . As for Leshem, who co-founded a startup that was acquired for $625 million in 2025, she also brings 11 years of experience in the military and intelligence field to their approach.

“Everything changed on October 7,” Leshem told TechCrunch. She was deployed, while pregnant, as a reservist on the day of the attacks. “And basically until the delivery room, I was there, witnessing and getting the first-row seat to how the battlefield acted differently from what I knew in the past decade.”

Protego won’t have the field to itself for long. Israeli authorities have taken notice of the same shift, awarding VC firms Adir Capital and Sling Capital about $33 million in state guarantees to invest in military and dual-use technologies, with other funds also raising capital for similar bets. (Leshem said Protego was too far along in its own fundraising to take part in the government’s tender.)

Protego, meanwhile, is already planning its next move: a second fund in the first quarter of 2027, backed by Israeli institutional investors and one large U.S. commitment Leshem has already secured, with a broader scope that includes early-growth American defense-tech companies.

This story was updated to correct the amount Protego will invest in companies.

articles.title: Will Chinese AI companies slow down? A top House Democrat wants answers
articles.summary: Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) is asking Chinese AI companies and US intelligence officials to assess their own abilities to audit and respond to AI safety risks.
articles.body: As President Donald Trump prepares to meet tech and AI CEOs in Washington, Rep. Ro Khanna (D-CA) is calling for a treaty between the US and China to keep AI from wreaking havoc on the world. But wrangling leaders in both countries to take action could be a long shot. In letters shared exclusively with The Verge, Khanna — the top Democrat on the House Select Committee on China and a possible presidential contender — asked a US intelligence agency and Chinese AI companies whether they would be prepared for an incident like OpenAI agents’ hack of Hugging Face this summer. The companies included DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI, all of which are pursuing high-level artificial intelligence. American and Chinese interests “could not be more different on many issues,” Khanna writes in the letter to Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton, “but on this discrete concern, it benefits neither country for humanity to lose control of our destiny.” Khanna requests the Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI) assess how effectively the US might respond to an AI lab losing control of its bots — a scenario that’s become increasingly common in recent months. Alongside it, he asked the agency to evaluate the Chinese government’s approach to assessing catastrophic AI risks. The information, he says, will help Congress and eventually the White House craft an agreement with their Chinese counterparts. The letters to DeepSeek, Alibaba, and Moonshot AI ask for documentation about their efforts to achieve “superintelligence” and recursive self-improvement (RSI) — a milestone where AI systems can improve on themselves. He asks about any efforts to implement safeguards and “kill switches” for the technology, as well as whether the companies would commit to inspections by a non-governmental agency if a treaty were struck. The companies and ODNI did not immediately respond to requests for comment from The Verge. Khanna’s move follows a meeting between Chinese President Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump at the White House last week. Both men, he says, fail to recognize the risk and urgency around AI. “I think it was constructive that Trump and Xi Jinping at least agreed to talk about AI and have ongoing dialogue about it, but it is not nearly adequate,” Khanna told The Verge in an interview on Monday. He is also skeptical of a planned Tuesday meeting between the White House, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-LA), and several American tech executives. “I think it’s an effort to reassure the American people that these tech companies are going to be responsible, and it’s a branding exercise,” Khanna says. “But why should we trust companies that have a motive to maximize profits to be making the rules for what is safe? It’s not that they’re bad people, but would you trust the pharmaceutical executives to determine the rules for what drugs are safe?” Khanna ultimately seeks a US-China treaty banning RSI and monitoring frontier AI labs, but he recognizes that’s unlikely to happen anytime soon. Sen. Bernie Sanders (I-VT) has similarly called for an AI treaty between the countries, though Republicans like House China Committee Chair John Moolenaar (R-MI) have been skeptical the Chinese government would keep its end of the bargain. In the meantime, Khanna says he’d like a working group with experts from both countries to suggest safety recommendations and methods for ensuring compliance. But Trump and his allies have been resistant to most regulations or agreements. The morning of his meeting with Xi last week, Trump posted on Truth Social, “Super Intelligence (SI) will be a big topic of discussion, but I want to leave it exactly where it is. That is China’s position also.” Johnson said on Fox Business that he expected the conversation to revolve around striking “the right balance” of oversight without stifling innovation, warning against losing the AI race against China. Leading US AI companies, however, have called for the US to coordinate with China to slow down the pace of development In the letter to the Chinese AI companies, Khanna acknowledges they’re unlikely to respond in full. He said they didn’t respond to requests in an earlier letter asking for a commitment to slow down AI development alongside OpenAI and Anthropic. Khanna tells The Verge his goal is to “shame them” and “spark a debate” among Chinese AI companies about safety. While he’s critical of US AI firms too, he says, “at least they’re engaging in safety conversations.” Khanna remains confident the US will drive AI safety standards, in part because he believes many Chinese models are distilled from US models. And while world leaders may not recognize the threat, they’re “out of touch with the scientists and technologists in their own countries,” he says. “We need to get the technologists and the engineers who understand this really driving the debate, not CEOs who have a vested interest in making profits, and not politicians who lack a technical expertise and who are more concerned about power.” [Media: [Media:

articles.title: Reco raises $55M as AI agent security startups crowd the market | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The round builds on a $30 million fundraise in February, taking the company's total funding to $140 million.
articles.body:
Terms like “AI sprawl” have become common fare on tech social media and in thought leadership as enterprises start deploying AI agents en masse. But CISOs worried about securing swarms of agents suddenly operating across networks are likely finding themselves dealing with a new kind of sprawl: vendors offering to help.

Just a quick glance at public Crunchbase and PitchBook profiles turns up at least two dozen companies selling some form of AI agent security. Some vendors vet the tools agents use , while others try to help companies control what data their agents can reach . Some others, like CrowdStrike , are building detection and response controls on the devices agents run, and still others are focused on finding and resolving unapproved AI usage .

The products differ, of course, but their promises to discover and govern agents sound quite similar, involving knowledge graphs, continuous monitoring, runtime security, tool access, MCP vetting, and the like.

Some are even updating their products to join the bandwagon. Until last year, AI security startup Reco was mostly selling software to map and secure SaaS and AI platforms. Now, it’s repositioned around a broader solution that uses a context graph to connect agents to apps, people, accounts, and permissions, giving security teams a way to see what an agent can reach and cut off access it doesn’t need.

According to Reco’s co-founder and CEO Ofer Klein, the biggest change over the past year that spurred the startup to broaden its scope was that companies are building and deploying AI agents faster than they can keep track of. At one of the startup’s Fortune 100 customers, he said, Reco’s platform found 21,000 agents the company didn’t know about. And at a large financial services customer, the startup claims it identified an agent set up by an ex-employee that could access Salesforce and share that data with a domain the company couldn’t see.

“The market demand right now for agent security is not only about the agent itself; it’s about the entire ecosystem end-to-end,” Klein told TechCrunch in an exclusive interview.

Klein’s not alone in stressing the urgency for companies to secure this sprawl. Security startup HiddenLayer ‘s co-founder and CEO, Chris Sestito, earlier this month told me that when agents reach production, the scale of their costs and risk goes from theoretical to “full scale really quickly,” and that over 50 of his customers have AI agents in production touching critical systems and sensitive assets.

Cymphony, another AI startup, said at one U.S. public company, it found about 85,000 files that had become accessible to AI tools and agents.

There’s no doubt a ton of investors are interested in companies that can make a mint out of helping companies find and secure all these agents, and Reco has capitalized on that demand: The startup on Tuesday said it raised $55 million, building on a $30 million Series B in February . AT&T, a customer, invested in the extension via its venture arm, as did Forestay and Quadrille Capital.

Klein said the company’s valuation has “more than doubled” since the Series B was first announced in February, and vaguely estimated it in the “high hundreds of millions” though he wouldn’t share specifics. Annual recurring revenue right now is in the “double-digit millions of dollars,” he said, and he expects it to triple this year. The startup has more than 100 customers, and financial services companies account for about 40% of the business.

Reco’s bet, it appears, is that its existing coverage of SaaS apps, and the AI agents they are increasingly offering, will help it stand out from the crowd. The company currently integrates with more than 280 apps, and Klein says new integrations can be added within days. Klein said the platform uses browser and network signals to find agents outside apps it connects to directly within companies, and it has controls to inspect prompts and tool calls.

The startup will use the new funding for hiring, sales, partnerships, and customer support. The new funding brings Reco’s total capital raised to $140 million.

articles.title: Navy aviators eject during carrier landing off Virginia
articles.summary: Two Navy aviators ejected on Monday as they landed their plane off the Virginia coast, with four sailors aboard the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower injured, according to the U.S. military. In a “mishap” that occurred at roughly 6:18 p.m. EDT during aircraft recovery operations, the two aviators assigned to Carrier Air Wing 3 ejected from…
articles.body:
Two Navy aviators ejected on Monday as they landed their plane off the Virginia coast, with four sailors aboard the USS Dwight D. Eisenhower injured, according to the U.S. military.

In a “mishap” that occurred at roughly 6:18 p.m. EDT during aircraft recovery operations, the two aviators assigned to Carrier Air Wing 3 ejected from their aircraft and were recovered by search-and-rescue personnel, the Navy said in a statement .

“Both aviators were safely returned to the ship and are being evaluated by medical personnel,” officials added.

Four individuals on board the carrier were injured during the incident, and one sailor was transported to a hospital in the Norfolk, Va., area for treatment of “non-life-threatening injuries,” per the branch.

The Nimitz-class Eisenhower is the flagship for the Navy’s Carrier Strike Group 2 , led by Rear Adm. P. Scott Miller. The five-star carrier has maritime security, expeditionary power projection, forward naval presence, crisis response and sea control capabilities.

Named for former President Eisenhower, the carrier’s home port is in Norfolk. The ship, which was commissioned in 1977 as only the second boat in the Nimitz class, deployed in support of U.S. military efforts in the Gulf War and the wars in Afghanistan and Iraq.

Another Nimitz-class carrier, the USS Theodore Roosevelt, departed Sunday from San Diego to relieve the USS George Washington in the Middle East.

The U.S. war with Iran , which hit the seven-month mark on Monday, has continued with no public sign of a deal to end hostilities.

President Trump on Monday reiterated his position that Iran “cannot have a nuclear weapon,” saying gas prices will decline once the conflict ends.

“I went to war to stop … one of the worst things that could happen to the world,” he told reporters in the Oval Office.

articles.title: Firefox just got a redesign with round tabs, new themes, and Compact Mode

articles.body: Firefox will look a little different the next time you launch it — more bubbly, with some new pops of color. The browser’s latest update brings a design overhaul to all desktop and mobile users, aimed at modernizing Firefox with bubble-like tabs, a rounded address bar, and refreshed colors, icons, and themes. The desktop and mobile versions of the browser will also now share the same design language. According to Mozilla, the design changes will have “no cost to your browser performance.” [Image: [Image: [Image: Mozilla says the overhauled design is a “renewal” for Firefox, following major updates over the last year, like homepage widgets, Split View, a built-in VPN, and controls for disabling the browser’s AI features. Firefox isn’t avoiding AI, though — it also launched its Smart Window AI mode earlier this year, which could help it compete with rivals’ AI browser features, like those in Chrome. With its rounded UI elements, Firefox now visually resembles Chrome a bit more, too. The design revamp also introduces more customization options, including more themes and wallpapers to choose from. Mozilla shared a peek at some of the updated theme options in May, including a dozen different colors to choose from, each with a light and dark mode. Along with the design overhaul, Firefox 157 brings the return of an old feature: Compact Mode, back after user requests. This condensed version of Firefox “reduces the size of your tabs and toolbar to give more of your screen to the web, with an auto-compact option for smaller screens.”

articles.title: Still running iOS 26? Update your iPhones, iPads and Macs for this urgent security fix | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Apple says the bug was used to attack "specific targeted individuals" running iOS 26, which the majority of Apple customers are still using.
articles.body:
Apple has fixed a security vulnerability in its iOS 26, iPadOS 26 and macOS 26 operating systems that the company says “may have been exploited” by hackers. The tech giant said the now-fixed bug could be used to launch “an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals on versions of iOS before iOS 27.”

According to a listing on Apple’s security pages , the bug was found in the main graphics engine that powers the user interface and visuals on iPhones, iPads and Macs.

Meta’s product security team was credited with the discovery.

Details of the bug, officially classed as CVE-2026-86950, were not released, but a device’s graphics engine typically has broad access to the rest of the device’s operating system. A successful exploit could potentially allow a hacker to steal a broad range of personal data from an affected device.

When reached by TechCrunch, spokespeople for Apple and Meta did not provide comment about how the bug was discovered, or how many people had their devices hacked due to this vulnerability, if any. It’s also unclear who may be exploiting the bug, such as government spyware makers or cybercriminals.

While the bug affects Apple’s previous generation of operating systems, it remains in wide usage. Almost four-in-five of Apple’s iPhone owners are still running iOS 26, according to the company’s own statistics . Devices running the latest version, iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, released earlier this month, also received a software update on Tuesday, but are unaffected by the bug under attack.

News of the security patch comes soon after Apple fixed another critical security bug, known as CVE-2026-86869, which could have allowed hackers to silently steal data from affected iPhones, iPads, or Macs.

Belgian cybersecurity research firm ironPeak published a detailed writeup last week explaining that the bug was a “zero-click” vulnerability that could be invisibly triggered via a maliciously crafted iMessage, without the user’s knowledge. Such bugs require no interaction from the victim, such as clicking a link, and are highly sought-after by surveillance vendors and spyware makers.

Per ironPeak’s post, the bug is capable of bypassing BlastDoor , a security feature that Apple implemented to prevent malicious code, like spyware, from escaping iMessage’s sandbox and hacking the user’s device.

Apple fixed the bug in September with the release of iOS 27, iPadOS 27, and macOS 27, and credited ironPeak’s Niels Hofmans with the discovery, alongside security researchers at Meta who confirmed their findings in a post on X .

It’s not yet known if this bug had been used in cyberattacks before it was fixed.

articles.title: Permanent daylight saving time expands in Canada: ‘Gives residents what they’ve asked us for’
articles.summary: (NEXSTAR) – Even more clocks across Canada will not “fall back” in November as permanent daylight saving time becomes the standard. Last week, officials in the Northwest Territories announced they would no longer observe seasonal time change. It came less than a week after Manitoba officials said daylight saving time would become permanent. In both…
articles.body:
(NEXSTAR) – Even more clocks across Canada will not “fall back” in November as permanent daylight saving time becomes the standard.

Last week, officials in the Northwest Territories announced they would no longer observe seasonal time change. It came less than a week after Manitoba officials said daylight saving time would become permanent.

In both cases, the government pointed to survey responses from residents.

“We heard from Manitobans loud and clear – no more changing the clocks in Manitoba,” Premier Wab Kinew said in a press release . Ninety-two percent of the nearly 72,000 residents who participated in Manitoba’s survey said they wanted the seasonal time change to end. Nearly 60% of those surveyed expressed support for permanent daylight saving time.

Of the more than 3,500 residents of the Northwest Territories who participated in a similar online survey, more than 87% said they wanted to stop changing the clocks twice a year. Once again, officials said permanent daylight saving time was the preferred option for locking the clocks.

“Ending seasonal time change gives residents what they’ve asked us for,” R.J. Simpson, Premier of the Northwest Territories, said in a press release.

Earlier this year, Alberta and British Columbia also switched to permanent daylight saving time. The latter said, in part, that “actions from the U.S. have shifted how [British Columbia] approaches decisions that merit alignment, including on time zones.”

Yukon and most of Saskatchewan have, for years, not observed the twice-annual changing of the clocks.

Nineteen U.S. states , including five that share a border with Canada, have enacted legislation calling for their clocks to lock on permanent daylight saving time. It has yet to happen for any of them, however.

States can opt into year-round permanent standard time , as Hawaii and much of Arizona have done , but they need action by Congress to observe permanent daylight saving time. Legislation has been introduced in the House to allow states to lock their clocks on year-round daylight saving time, but the chamber won’t be back in session until November .

The House passed the Sunshine Protection Act earlier this year, and President Trump has expressed his support for the bill. It’s not clear if or when the Senate could take up the bill, or if it has enough votes to pass .

Without any major changes, U.S. clocks will “fall back” to standard time on November 1, the earliest possible date daylight saving time can end.

articles.title: OpenAI halts releasing newest model over safety concerns
articles.summary: OpenAI on Monday halted the release of its newest artificial intelligence model over safety concerns as tech companies grapple with potential risks as a result of more advanced AI software. Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, told The New York Times that the new model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, “didn’t quite meet the bar in…
articles.body:
OpenAI on Monday halted the release of its newest artificial intelligence model over safety concerns as tech companies grapple with potential risks as a result of more advanced AI software.

Saachi Jain, OpenAI’s head of safety systems, told The New York Times that the new model, called GPT-6.1 Astra, “didn’t quite meet the bar in terms of staying within scope authorization, and how it communicates back to the user about the type of work it’s done.”

The Hill has reached out to OpenAI for comment.

The company told the Times that the new model was prone to high levels of deception and willing to mislead users about its actions, as well as going beyond what a user initially asks it.

Jain also noted to The Associated Press that OpenAI was committed to ensuring the model was safe either during testing or when handled by a user. It is expected to be integrated into ChatGPT and Codex, designed to handle tasks that are more complex and without human assistance.

Placing the new model’s release on hold follows growing concerns about rogue AI software attempting to hack, or successfully hack , government websites and data. OpenAI said last week that its technology accessed parts of the Department of Education website and improperly interacted with websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) and the U.S. Census Bureau.

OpenAI CEO Sam Altman was among several tech company heads to speak at the United Nations General Assembly last week, urging world leaders to act in response to advancing AI software.

“We have a choice in front of us,” he said in his address . “AI can either be more like a new Renaissance of creativity and discovery, or more like a new Industrial Revolution of upheaval and disarray.”

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill have also called for stricter regulations on AI, responding to potential security risks and AI’s possible existential threat to humanity. Former OpenAI and Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon warned earlier this month that AI could bring the end of humanity by the end of the decade.

Among those calling for stronger safeguards and dismissing claims that the rapidly developing tech’s potential risks are “fake news” was Pope Leo XIV, who said AI should be “ taken seriously .”

“We need to continue to invite political leaders, leaders of AI, social organizations, associations to come together and look at what is happening already and what could be down the road,” he told reporters Monday.

“To simply say, ‘Oh, it’s not going to happen,’ and close our eyes to it, I think is probably not the most responsible way to go about that,” the pontiff added.

articles.title: Court blocks Trump bid to withhold some counterterrorism funds for states that don’t adopt election reforms
articles.summary: A federal court has blocked the Trump administration’s efforts to withhold some counterterrorism funding from states that do not adopt election reforms favored by the administration. Earlier this year, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), which administers the grants, said that states and localities will have to adopt five election policies — including the use…
articles.body:
A federal court has blocked the Trump administration’s efforts to withhold some counterterrorism funding from states that do not adopt election reforms favored by the administration.

Earlier this year, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA), which administers the grants, said that states and localities will have to adopt five election policies — including the use of a controversial database to check the citizenship status of voters — or the administration would withhold 20 percent of the funds.

On Monday, Judge Amir Ali, an appointee of former President Biden, determined the move to withhold some of the money goes beyond FEMA’s statutory authority.

“The statute gives FEMA the authority to fund projects proposed by states and high-risk urban areas; it does not give FEMA authority to use the possibility of grants to induce states or high-risk urban areas to carry out the federal government’s preferred projects at their own expense,” Ali wrote.

The grant programs in question are known as the Urban Area Security Initiative and State Homeland Security Grant Program, the former of which helps cities in particular respond to terror threats. They were created after 9/11 to help prevent attacks.

“Election security is national security, and protecting critical infrastructure remains a top priority for the Trump Administration,” Victoria Barton, associate administrator at FEMA’s Office of External Affairs, said in a statement to The Hill. “FEMA is reviewing the court’s decision and will comply with the court’s order. The ruling does not affect FEMA’s broader mission to support state and local partners in preventing, preparing for, protecting against, and responding to terrorism, including through eligible physical and cybersecurity investments that protect election infrastructure.”

Earlier this year, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the move as protecting election security and ensuring that Americans can trust the results of their elections.

“Under President Trump’s leadership, we are taking decisive action to protect election systems from threats like foreign interference, insider threats, and cyberattacks. These new requirements for homeland security grant recipients will preserve election integrity and ensure that Americans can trust the results,” Mullin said in July.

However, critics see the policy as a backdoor way to force states to check the citizenship status of voters, something Trump has also tried to do through executive action.

In particular, the policy would have forced states to use U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services’s Systematic Alien Verification for Entitlements to verify citizenship.

The database, which is traditionally used to verify whether someone is eligible for programs like food stamps and other entitlements, has been criticized for being out of date and otherwise containing faulty information.

Zach Schonfeld and Rebecca Beitsch contributed.

articles.title: FBI strikes back at hacking group with overseas arrest of alleged leader
articles.summary: A 24-year-old Amsterdam man was arrested by Dutch police and the FBI for allegedly leading the ShinyHunters global hacking syndicate network.
articles.body: An alleged leader of the notorious global hacking syndicate ShinyHunters has been arrested in the Netherlands following a joint operation between the FBI and Dutch authorities, targeting a cybercrime network linked to high-profile attacks across the U.S. and worldwide. Dutch police announced the arrest of a 24-year-old Amsterdam man Sept. 15 for his alleged role in the ShinyHunters hacking group and for attempting to incite two murders, with authorities noting that further arrests remain possible as they investigate seized electronic devices. "This morning @FBI and our partners the Dutch National Police are announcing the arrest of one of the alleged leaders of ShinyHunters – a global cybercrime and threat actor group linked to cyberattacks in the United States, the Netherlands, and around the world," FBI Director Kash Patel wrote Tuesday morning on X. FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS "In coordination with FBI investigators the Dutch High-Tech Crime Unit arrested the suspect under Dutch law. As we speak FBI teams are actively working with partners to obtain and execute more leads in the ongoing investigation based on this arrest. "Thank you to our Dutch National Police partners for their continued work with us in this case and the industry partners who shared information with us. The investigation continues." "The man is also suspected of attempted incitement to commit two murders," according to a Dutch police release. "Various data carriers have been seized and are being investigated further. Further arrests are not ruled out." Brett Leatherman, assistant director of ​the FBI's ⁠Cyber Division, made an unusually public address to the hacking group ShinyHunters, telling the cybercriminals that "we know how to find you." FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS "To the remaining members of ShinyHunters: You've heard about the arrest of your colleague," Leatherman's video statement warned. "We're confident you've seen or heard things in recent days that the public has not."Other groups believed anonymity or their friends would protect them, and they were wrong. Arrests have a way of changing who is willing to talk. And seized infrastructure has a way of showing us who's left."The longer you stay in this, the more we learn about you. You know how to find us and we know how find you. I suggest you reach out first while the choice is still yours." Benjamin Korper of Amsterdam-based cybersecurity company Neo Security named the arrested man as Pepijn van der Stap, the company's offensive security lead. FBI EXTRADITES CHINESE HACKER ACCUSED OF STEALING COVID-19 RESEARCH "Since last year, this cyber criminal and his co-conspirators have allegedly breached more than 140 organizations and taken at least $70 million in extortion payments," Leatherman said in his video statement, which did not name the suspect. "They often target third-party vendors and cloud-based platforms, stealing sensitive data in extorting victims with threats to publish it."In a telephone interview with Reuters, Korper said Dutch forensic investigators visited his office Sept. 15, the night Van der Stap was arrested in a dramatic police raid that involved flash bang grenades. ShinyHunters is a hacking group known for large-scale data breaches and extortion and had announced its recent theft of what it said was terabytes of sensitive personnel data from U.S. FBI servers, including intelligence assignments and medical records of employees, according to Reuters. An internal memo circulated to staffers said the FBI was operating under the presumption that hackers stole data pertaining to all bureau employees, a source told Reuters. FBI SAYS SOURCE OF ITS JOBS PORTAL BREACH STILL UNKNOWN AS HACKERS ALLEGE EMPLOYEE DATA COMPROMISED In a statement, ShinyHunters said Van der Stap had "no association" with the group and that Dutch police were incompetent. News of Van der Stap's arrest caused a stir in the cybersecurity community. Van der Stap's 2023 convictions of data theft and extortion had already received widespread publicity, as did his subsequent public disavowal of cybercrime. On his personal website, Van der Stap acknowledged his journey "hasn't been a straight line" but said his experience had taught him that "knowledge is for building and protecting, not breaking." Korper said he had carefully vetted Van der Stap before hiring him, monitored him during his employment, and was shocked by the arrest. "I truly believe that people deserve a second chance, but in this case I was not thanked for it," Korper said. "Absolutely everybody I talked to is flabbergasted." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP The executive said he had hired an outside firm to investigate whether Van der Stap had hacked Neo Security or its customers, but so far investigators have found no evidence that he acted against his employer or its clients. Korper and Van der Stap have not been in touch since the arrest, Korper said. Reuters contributed to this report.

articles.title: New Mexico venture studio unveils quantum lab to boost US tech edge
articles.summary: The investment and incubation firm Roadrunner Venture Studios will unveil a new quantum lab Tuesday in Albuquerque as New Mexico looks to bolster the U.S.’s position in the global race for quantum computing. The Roadrunner Quantum Lab will open as part of the state’s $450 million commitment to quantum development. Those behind the project say…
articles.body:
The investment and incubation firm Roadrunner Venture Studios will unveil a new quantum lab Tuesday in Albuquerque as New Mexico looks to bolster the U.S.’s position in the global race for quantum computing.

The Roadrunner Quantum Lab will open as part of the state’s $450 million commitment to quantum development. Those behind the project say it will provide the capital, infrastructure and national lab research for firms to work towards commercializing quantum computing, according to details first shared with The Hill.

The 35,000-square-foot lab will first open its doors to eight quantum companies, Sandia National Laboratories, Los Alamos National Laboratories and the Quantum New Mexico Institute.

“In a national lab setting, you don’t have that mix,” Adam Hammer, the co-founder and CEO of Roadrunner Venture Studios, told The Hill on Monday. “You have a lot of researchers. You might have some recruitment, but you don’t have capital. In the private sector setting, you have, maybe the capital, but you certainly don’t have the infrastructure that’s required, and oftentimes you don’t have access to the talent.”

Unlike traditional computing, which relies on bits or pieces of data that are either a zero or one, quantum computers use qubits, which can be both zero and one at the same time.

Using the laws of physics, quantum computing can solve complex problems much faster than classical computers. Like AI, quantum computing can be used as a defensive tool, but it can also give bad actors the ability to quickly untangle the encryption that protects computers.

The technology is still in an experimental or research phase, but practical use and commercialization is next.

“When we think about this from a policy angle, quantum is going to be one of the big battlegrounds between the U.S. and China and we’re seeing this take shape today,” Hammer said. “A lot of conversation taking shape globally is how the United States and China are positioning around this new era of compute.”

On AI, “there are elements that China has done really well. Think about even power generation from an infrastructure layer, the United States lags, China’s ahead, but when we think about chip development, we’re ahead,” he said.

“We are ahead in quantum technologies, but not that far ahead,” he continued. “And what we have to do to win in this space is not to do a bunch of great [research and development], it’s to build great products,” Hammer added.

The Trump administration has made quantum computing a priority for the U.S. government. President Trump signed a pair of executive orders in June, one of which sets a goal of moving certain government computing systems to post-quantum cryptography by 2030 or 2031. It also urges the Pentagon to use quantum sensors by 2028.

Rob Black, New Mexico’s secretary of Economic Development, emphasized the state has long been a leader in research and development — from the start of Microsoft to the Manhattan Project — but it has not hosted most commercialization of tech.

“Certainly, we have Intel here, we have other things, and we have lab spaces,” Black told The Hill in an interview Monday. “But when you think about the commercialization of a lot of the technologies that came out of Sandia and LANL Air Force Research Lab, the work that’s been done here, those economic benefits have translated into Seattle, into other places.”

“So we’re taking a major bet into the sector because we believe again we have a right to win this for the U.S. and for our country,” Black said.

New Mexico hosts the nation’s second-largest state sovereign wealth fund of about $75 billion. About $2 billion of this fund is being put into 30 of the “best venture capital” firms in the world to invest in the state, Black said.

The state is home to the University of New Mexico’s Quantum Institute, where about 60 doctorates specialized in quantum information sciences have graduated.

“From a talent perspective, it’s the highest Ph.D. per capita of any state in America,” Hammer said, explaining the decision to build the lab in New Mexico.

The eight firms that will first get access to the lab are Diraq, IonQ, Quantum Machines, Conductor Quantum, Mesa Quantum, QBoltz, Photon Queue and Quera.

articles.title: Hegseth to cut 20 percent of admirals, generals in major Pentagon overhaul
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is set to announce a 20 percent cut to slots slated for admirals and generals at the Pentagon as part of his push to overhaul the outlook of the department, two Pentagon officials confirmed to The Hill on Tuesday. The Defense secretary will publicize the reductions, which will affect senior leadership…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is set to announce a 20 percent cut to slots slated for admirals and generals at the Pentagon as part of his push to overhaul the outlook of the department, two Pentagon officials confirmed to The Hill on Tuesday.

The Defense secretary will publicize the reductions, which will affect senior leadership positions across the Army, Navy and the Air Force, on Wednesday during his State of the Force address in Quantico, Va., the officials said.

The Pentagon chief will address junior officers and enlisted leaders at the Marine Corps base, where he will outline his priorities for the Pentagon in the coming months, including the major leadership shake-up.

The new push from the Defense secretary comes after he looked to cut the number of active-duty four-star generals and admirals in the U.S. military by at least 10 percent last year.

In May 2025, Hegseth directed Pentagon leadership to cut the number of general officers in the National Guard by at least 20 percent and slash the total number of general and flag officers — those with a one-star rank or above — by 10 percent.

The Pentagon chief’s May order said he wanted “Less Generals, more GIs” and to “shift resources from bloated headquarters elements to our warfighters.”

Hegseth argued at the time the reductions were critical to remove “redundant force structure to optimize and streamline leadership by reducing excess general and flag officer positions.”

The forthcoming announcement was first reported by Fox News Digital. The service branches are requested to implement the cuts by Jan. 1, while some positions will be downgraded instead of slashed, according to memos reviewed by Fox.

The Pentagon is requiring troops to meet waist-to-height requirements and exhibit “impeccable” grooming standards to attend Hegseth’s speech on Wednesday.

The upcoming leadership cuts come as Hegseth has fired or pushed out more than two dozen military leaders across the military branches since taking the leading role at the Pentagon, personnel moves that have unnerved congressional lawmakers in both parties .

In July, Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), the chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee, said she was concerned by the removal of senior military officers and blocking promotions of lower-ranked personnel.

“I find this deeply troubling,” Collins said during a hearing . “These are men and women who volunteered to serve our country and swore an oath to support and defend our Constitution.”

Rep. Austin Scott (R-Ga.), who sits on the House Armed Services Committee, said during an April hearing that Hegseth’s firing of Gen. Randy George, the U.S. Army’s former chief of staff, would have a “chilling effect” on the way the armed services operate.

The Pentagon chief has also blocked promotions of officers slated for promotion to one- and two-star generals, saying that military leaders serve at the pleasure of the president.

articles.title: Schumer slams data center bill as ‘ineffectual participation trophy’
articles.summary: Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Tuesday slammed a bill that would force states to consider standards to mitigate data centers’ power price impacts as an “ineffectual participation trophy.” His comments signal that Democrats could try to block the bill, which the Senate is expected to take up this week. “Americans are demanding real…
articles.body:
Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) on Tuesday slammed a bill that would force states to consider standards to mitigate data centers’ power price impacts as an “ineffectual participation trophy.”

His comments signal that Democrats could try to block the bill, which the Senate is expected to take up this week.

“Americans are demanding real guardrails on AI and data centers, but all the Republicans offer is a toothless messaging bill. The bill is a fraud. I can sum up the shortcomings of the Republican data center bill with one word: optional. The bill is optional,” Schumer said in a speech on the Senate floor.

“At a time when Americans are calling out for real guardrails on AI, Senate Republicans are trying to secure an ineffectual participation trophy before they skip town. Instead of trying to score cheap political points with hollow proposals, Senate Republicans need to work with us to take meaningful action that will actually contain these existential risks.”

The legislation in question, known as the Ratepayer Protection Act, overwhelmingly passed the House in a bipartisan vote.

However, it has met some criticism, including from lawmakers who supported it, for not doing enough.

It would require states to hold hearings on standards to force data centers to pay for extra electric infrastructure needed to power their facilities. But it wouldn’t make the states adopt any standards — so states that don’t want to act ultimately would not have to.

Sen. Jon Husted (R-Ohio), who faces a tough reelection battle in November, recently attempted to pass the bill unanimously through the Senate but was blocked by Sen. Martin Heinrich (D-N.M.).

The bill’s ultimate fate is not clear, as seven Democrats would need to join Republicans in voting for it to cross the Senate’s 60-vote threshold.

articles.title: Cruz blocks push by Democrats to unanimously pass AI safety bill
articles.summary: Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) blocked an effort by Democrats on Tuesday to pass legislation creating an AI safety panel tasked with evaluating and creating enforceable standards for frontier models. Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee, objected to an attempt by Sens. Mark Warner (D-Va.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) and Andy Kim (D-N.J.) to pass the…
articles.body:
Sen. Ted Cruz (R-Texas) blocked an effort by Democrats on Tuesday to pass legislation creating an AI safety panel tasked with evaluating and creating enforceable standards for frontier models.

Cruz, who chairs the Senate Commerce Committee, objected to an attempt by Sens. Mark Warner (D-Va.), Brian Schatz (D-Hawaii) and Andy Kim (D-N.J.) to pass the measure by unanimous consent on the Senate floor.

Their bill, the Artificial Intelligence Risk Management and Security Act of 2026, aims to establish a permanent AI Safety Board within the Commerce Department. But Cruz said he had concerns that the proposal would give the executive branch too much power over private AI companies.

The board would develop standards for evaluating frontier models and securing their testing environments, with developers required to give the panel access to models at least 45 days before they go public. They could face fines for failing to comply with the board’s standards.

“We can’t, frankly, have regular business at this moment,” Warner said from the Senate floor on Tuesday, as he sought to bypass a standard floor vote with unanimous consent.

“I remain an AI optimist,” he added. “I am not an AI doomer. But we are at a moment in time, particularly over the last few weeks, where I think the whole world has recognized that we’ve got to do something.”

The push comes as several prominent AI leaders have called for a slowdown in development and urged the federal government to create safeguards amid concerns about the technology’s risks to humanity.

A series of recent incidents are putting AI safety issues front and center . Over the past few months, agents from several major AI companies have hacked into other firms — and in at least one case, an Australian health agency.

OpenAI also reportedly halted the release of its newest AI model Monday over safety concerns.

“My judgment is that we don’t have the luxury of time,” Schatz said Tuesday. “The Senate is supposed to be the cooling saucer that allows the hot liquid from the House to cool off, and then we can deliberate, right?”

“Well, the House is out of town, and they did not send us anything to drink,” he continued. “And so that’s a lovely way to understand this body, but we’re all that’s left, and we have to work on a nonpartisan, forget bipartisan, a nonpartisan basis to make sure that humans remain in control of the technology.”

However, Cruz said he still has “real reservations about this specific proposal,” suggesting it would give broad authorities to the executive branch by allowing it to pick the AI safety board that ultimately sets the rules for developers.

“These terms are not bound by existing statutes or traditional legal doctrines, or even further defined,” he said. “That concerns me, because it is difficult to imagine what an ambitious bureaucrat couldn’t shoehorn under this broad authority.”

“I would be more than happy to work with the sponsors on approaches that do not offer such unbound discretion to the federal government and that are not an invitation for abuse,” Cruz added.

articles.title: Trump to sign order renaming AI as ‘superintelligence’
articles.summary: President Trump plans to sign an order Tuesday officially renaming AI as “superintelligence.” “We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence because it’s not artificial,” Trump said in public remarks, after hosting a luncheon with top technology executives at the White House. “We all agree on that, and…
articles.body:
President Trump plans to sign an order Tuesday officially renaming AI as “superintelligence.”

“We’re going to be signing a document today at about 5 o’clock, renaming artificial intelligence because it’s not artificial,” Trump said in public remarks, after hosting a luncheon with top technology executives at the White House.

“We all agree on that, and we’re going to be renaming it superintelligence, officially renaming it,” he continued.

Trump has been pushing to rebrand AI in recent weeks. He initially floated several new names for the technology before settling on superintelligence, declaring at the United Nations that official U.S. documents would use the term going forward.

Notably, superintelligence is already a defined term, referring to AI that goes beyond human intelligence.

“The use of the word ‘artificial’ makes intelligence sound fake,” Trump said last week. “It is not fake. It’s actually amazing. But we have to be careful. In fact, it is exactly the opposite of what it purports.”

His focus on renaming AI comes amid widespread concerns about the technology’s risks. Researchers have warned in recent weeks that AI could threaten humanity, prompting calls from key tech leaders for a slowdown in development.

However, Trump has repeatedly dismissed safety concerns, arguing that the U.S. needs to power ahead to maintain its lead over China on AI.

articles.title: Hegseth freezes hiring of civilian tenured faculty at US military academies
articles.summary: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed departments on Tuesday to halt appointments of civilian staff to tenured positions at U.S. military service academies and develop hiring plans that prioritize “institutional flexibility and faculty contribution to the warfighting mission.” “The primary purpose of our Military Service Academies (MSA) is to prepare the next generation of officers to…
articles.body:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth directed departments on Tuesday to halt appointments of civilian staff to tenured positions at U.S. military service academies and develop hiring plans that prioritize “institutional flexibility and faculty contribution to the warfighting mission.”

“The primary purpose of our Military Service Academies (MSA) is to prepare the next generation of officers to lead the men and women of the greatest military on Earth. To ensure our educational institutions remain firmly focused on this warfighting mission, we must address the structural mechanisms that have allowed civilian academic norms to dilute our focus on lethality,” Hegseth said in a one-page memo titled “Refocusing the Military Service Academies on Warfighter Education.”

The Pentagon chief said in the memo that granting tenure to civilian faculty “often leads to academic stagnation, faculty complacency and institutional inability to adapt to emerging needs.”

“Additionally, it contributes to curriculum that drifts from the mission of educating our warfighters to the research priorities of the tenured academics,” Hegseth said.

CBS News reported in July the Pentagon was weighing a move to end civilian tenure at military academies.

The U.S. has five service academies: West Point in New York, U.S. Naval Academy in Maryland, Air Force Academy in Colorado, Coast Guard Academy in Connecticut and Merchant Marine Academy in New York.

The Coast Guard Academy resides under the Department of Homeland Security, while the Merchant Marine Academy is under the Department of Transportation’s Maritime Administration.

West Point said it has 27 percent civilian faculty. The U.S. Naval Academy has 217 tenured civilian professors and 67 civilian professors on tenure track. An Air Force Academy “Academic FAQ” page previously said the school has about 70 percent military instructors and 30 percent civilians.

It wasn’t immediately clear whether currently tenured faculty would be impacted by the order.

The memo is part of Hegseth’s push to overhaul military service academies. The Pentagon chief said last year his goal was to get “woke” civilian professors out of the institutions and replace them with military personnel.

“We need more uniformed members going back into West Point, the Air Force Academy, the Naval Academy as a tour to teach with their wisdom of what they’ve learned in uniform instead of just more civilian professors that came from the same left-wing, woke universities that they left and then try to push that into service academies,” the Defense secretary said during his confirmation hearing.

Earlier this year, Hegseth rolled out a new task force — led by Anthony Tata, undersecretary of Defense for personnel and readiness — to conduct a review of U.S. war colleges to make sure they are “effective” and focused on critical national security issues.

Some of those schools being assessed are Army War College, National Defense University, the Naval War College, Marine Corps University and the Air War College.

“We want military leaders who are critical thinkers that have studied the principles on which our founding fathers established this republic, and that are educated and prepared to win wars,” Hegseth said in March.

articles.title: What would Jon Husted’s data center bill actually do?
articles.summary: Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) Ratepayer Protection Act aims to mitigate high electricity costs associated with data centers, but even if it passes, it’s not clear if the bill would have any impact. The legislation, which easily cleared the House 417-3, requires states and some electric utilities to consider a standard under which data centers would…
articles.body:
Sen. Jon Husted’s (R-Ohio) Ratepayer Protection Act aims to mitigate high electricity costs associated with data centers, but even if it passes, it’s not clear if the bill would have any impact.

The legislation, which easily cleared the House 417-3 , requires states and some electric utilities to consider a standard under which data centers would have to pay for additional costs caused by their large power demand.

It does not require the adoption of any such standards, saying it would be up to the states or the nonregulated utilities to decide whether they want to take up any such standard. They would have two years to make that decision.

Experts and electricity rate advocates have told The Hill in recent weeks that the bill could be a step toward mitigating data centers’ electricity costs by forcing states that are not already doing anything to at least weigh a change in policy.

“There are states that are not addressing this issue as proactively … so having a message from Congress that says, ‘Hey, you, within this timeline, need to at least take up this issue,’ is a good push,” Clara Summers, director of the Consumers for a Better Grid Campaign at Citizens Utility Board, told The Hill in July .

Allison Clements, former commissioner of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, said that for some states, the bill’s requirements could be redundant of what they are already directed to do by a recent commission order .

“Is it a good step? Yes. Is it anywhere close to sufficient relative to these challenges? No,” said Clements, a Democrat who is now principal at energy consulting firm 804 Advisory.

While it passed with flying colors in the House, the bill is expected to hit Democratic resistance in the Senate, where several lawmakers have criticized it as not doing very much.

“It’s got no teeth in it,” Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.) told The Hill on Tuesday.

Husted, meanwhile, has said the bill is important for ensuring “American families are not left footing the bill for energy infrastructure required by data centers.”

The Ohio Republican is locked in a tight Senate race against former Sen. Sherrod Brown (D-Ohio).

articles.body:
Cotton presses Hegseth to review supply chains after F-35 parts ended up in China

Sen. Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), the chairman of the Senate Intelligence Committee, pressed Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth on Tuesday to review the military supply chains after sensitive F-35 fighter jet parts were diverted to Hong Kong and are now in China’s possession.

“DOW relies extensively on contractors and commercial carriers to move military equipment, replacement parts, and vital supplies around the world. And while I recognize that such arrangements allow for ease and speed of movement, those advantages must not come at the expense of maintaining our military edge ,” Cotton wrote in a letter .

The Arkansas Republican, who also sits on the Senate Armed Services Committee (SASC), asked the Pentagon to review the chain-of-custody requirements for military equipment and parts shipped by contractors and commercial carriers, the department’s ability to track the location and routing of these shipments and procedures for allowing and reporting changes to routes.

Cotton also asked the Pentagon to examine “ safeguards to prevent military materiel from transiting through or being diverted to China and other adversary-controlled jurisdictions.”

“Classified and designated sensitive components should receive heightened protections, but all U.S. military material can provide adversaries valuable insight into U.S. weapons systems , logistics and readiness, as well as access to American troops,” Cotton continued.

When reached for comment, the Pentagon said, “as with all congressional correspondence, the Department will respond directly to the authors .”

The letter comes after reports that F-35 Lightning II components were diverted this summer to Hong Kong after being sent from Australia .

The parts, including the canopy and weapons-bay door , were included in the package shipped by UPS.

The development has sparked concerns among both Senate Democrats and Republicans , who have pressed the Pentagon to investigate the matter.

Sen. Deb Fischer (R-Neb.), who is also a SASC member, told reporters last week she is “very concerned” about China having possession of F-35 parts.

articles.title: Five things to know about Trump’s new AI website
articles.summary: President Trump launched America.gov on Tuesday, a website that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to help Americans find information across government websites with a single search. Trump said the website has been in the works since the early days of his second term and that it’s still a work in progress. The website’s unveiling took place…
articles.body:
President Trump launched America.gov on Tuesday, a website that uses artificial intelligence (AI) to help Americans find information across government websites with a single search.

Trump said the website has been in the works since the early days of his second term and that it’s still a work in progress. The website’s unveiling took place at the Andrew W. Mellon Auditorium in Washington, D.C. were industry leaders and administration officials participated in presentations and discussions.

“Whether you’re a scout leader who wants to reserve a campsite at a national park, a senior citizen trying to choose a Medicare plan, or an American veteran trying to get the benefits that you’ve earned and so justly deserve, America.gov will be there to help and to help you accurately and quickly,” Trump said in his speech at the event.

Here are five things to know about the AI-powered website:

The General Services Administration (GSA) engineered the platform in partnership with the National Design Studio, per a release from the agency. ​

U.S. Chief Design Officer Joe Gebbia told CNBC Tuesday ahead of the site’s launch that the website is powered by Google’s Gemini and Elon Musk’s Grok.

​“Hello, America,” the website says. “Whatever you need from government, start here.”

​The website states it is free to use with no ads, and no account is required. Under the frequently asked questions section, it says the website “does not provide campaign or party information.”

The acting director of Technology Transformation Services at GSA, Sam Corcos, is overseeing the project. He is a former member of Trump’s shuttered Department of Government Efficiency.

​Trump claimed Tuesday that the website “cannot, in theory, be hacked into,” noting that “everying is totally private” and “personal information is not collected or stored.”

Just government-related queries accepted

The website says it takes information from 29,000 websites, and all answers are “exclusively sourced from federal, state, and local websites.” It does not answer questions about politics, culture or health, for example.

“The accuracy of our answers is never influenced by third parties,” the website says.

Users can search a question by typing or via voice. The search bar on the website’s home page offers examples of possible questions: “How do I replace my Social Security card? “I just got married. How do I change my last name?” “When do I qualify for Medicare?”

Users can also attach a document, and the AI tool will aim to help make sense of the file. The website notes that detailed queries prompt more helpful responses.

“The more specific you get, the better we answer, right down to your dates, state, and circumstances,” it says.

Passport, name change applications available in 2027

The website is still new, but it says in 2027 that users will be able to apply for and renew passports online.

Secretary of State Marco Rubio laid out the process Tuesday. The site would allow an applicant to submit their information, upload a photo, and track its approval and shipment.

He said users will be able to see the photo in a mockup of a passport and can retake their photos.

“No printing forms, no drug store hostage photo, no appointment, no line, no middleman that you’re paying to do something that should be available to you,” Rubio said.

The website also says users will be able to update their legal name across all agencies.

The platform will also eventually allow users to enroll in Medicare and simplify the process.

Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Mehmet Oz showed how the website would work Tuesday.

He said the platform will also show users which providers in their area take Medicare, along with available appointment times. The site will also allow appointment bookings.

Oz said the site will also allow users to compare prescription coverage.

Job application tool in the pipeline too

The site will also allow users to upload resumes and apply to government positions in 2027, according to the administration.

For now, people can find and apply to federal jobs at USAJobs.gov .
